speechtext:
Sir WILFRID* LAURIER. I beg to move:
That from Monday next until the end of the session, the House shall meet on that and every subsequent sitting day at 11 o'clock in the morning and that, in addition to the usual intermission at six o'clock p.m., there shall also be an intermission from one to three o'clock in the afternoon.

I think there is no objection to the motion, as we all desire to bring the session to a close at a reasonably early date. It would, however, be desirable that the right hon. gentleman should state what further legislation, if any, the government proposes to submit this session.
Sir FREDERICK BORDEN

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We shall have some supplementary estimates, then a resolution to amend the law concerning dry-docks, also the renewal of some railway subsidies, but no new subsidies, and some legislation regarding the Otta-wa Improvement Commission, also legislation with regard to judicial appointments necessitated by legislation of the local legislatures. If there be anything else I shall inform the House on Monday.
Motion agreed to.

Hon. RODOLPHE LEMIEUX (Postmaster General) moved that on Monday next the House go into Committee of the Whole to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Civil Service Act, chapter 16 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, by providing for the payment of salaries as follows:-
To post office inspectors on appointment, $2,500, with an annual increase of $100 to a maximum of $3,500.
To assistant jiost office inspectors and superintendents of the railway mail service on appointment, $1,600, with an annual increase of $100 to a maximum of $2,500.
To authorize the increase to the minimum of the salary of any such officers whose salary is at present less than the minimum.
To assistant postmasters, on appointment, a salary of not less than $1,100 and not more than $2,800.
Motion agreed to.

Before the orders of the day are called, I would like to ask the right hon. the Prime Minister whether he has brought down the correspondence relating to the Waterways Treaty, which we have asked for?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It will be laid on the table Monday next.

TRADE NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. the Finance Minister to give me, at as early a date as possible, particulars of the goods that have been imported under item 711 of the present tariff, which is affected by the recent arrangements with the United States. I would like to have particulars of the goods imported from the United States under that item, the classes of goods embraced under that item generally speaking, and the expectations of the government with respect to the same, also particulars regarding changes anticipated in importations this as well as the other items.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TRADE NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: How these will affect the revenue?

maintopic: TRADE NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I was not thinking so much of the revenue, though of course that would be affected. There will be a smaller customs tax, but possibly a larger revenue. What I want more particularly is the actual volume of the importations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TRADE NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I am not sure that we can give the exact information, as that would be a good deal a matter of surmise. However, I shall endeavour, as far as possible, to give the information desired before we proceed further.

maintopic: TRADE NEGOTIATIONS WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Of course, information as to the revenue should in itself convey information as to the importations because the one depends on the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I have already given instructions to prepare a memorandum giving the probable reductions of taxation under the new arrangements. That memorandum should give all the information the hon. gentleman desires. At all events I shall do my best to-furnish it.

the amount of the expenditure, but we have a right to complain that an over expenditure was made last year as to which the judgment of the House was never invited.
["I am afraid I cannot let the hon. member proceed, as the House goes automatically into Committee of Supply, which was interrupted at six o'clock."]

We shall have to ask for a further amount this session.
Quebec harbour-deep-water wharf at Levis, $55,000.

We purpose constructing a deep water wharf on the property acquired from the Bank of Montreal, formerly the Carrier-Laine property. $400,000 was voted last year, and out of it we have paid for the property, and we think the vote of $55,000 will enable us to enter into a contract.
That will not complete the work?
Oh, no.
What is the work to cost?
I am informed by the chief engineer that the estimated cost is about $400,000. We purpose going to a depth of 35 feet at the end of the wharf.

You had a vote last year of $400,000; how was that expended?
House in Committee of Supply.
Port Arthur and Fort William harbour and river improvements, $800,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext: This is to make provision for improvements in the way of dredging on the Mission river, and also at the harbour of Port Arthur, and for revetment walls on the Mission river, and also for a breakwater at Port Arthur. This amount is required to carry on the work during the present year.
Under contract?
All under contract.
Will the minister have an over expenditure the same as last year?

In view of the rapidity with which the work is going ahead, and also in view of the fact that we have given favourable consideration to the proposal to build a breakwater extending from what is known as Bare-point, a little to the east, of the dry dock and ship-building and repairing plant, which are being established at Port Arthur, this amount will not be sufficient, and we propose asking for a further amount-if my colleagues approve of it-in the supplementary estimates. It is desirable to carry on this work without unnecessary delay.
If this improvement is needed I will not be found to grumble at

The expenditure was $355,000 as follows: Balance of purchase price paid to the Bank of Montreal, $330,000; interest at 5 per cent, $4,855.55; further interest at 5 per cent, $8,572.43; outlay for arbitration and surveying expenses and temporary repairs, $4,919.43; additional expenditure previous to the close of the fiscal year, $1,652.59.
Quebec harbour-improvements at mouth of River St. Charles' estuary, $180,000.

This work has been going on for a number of years with the object of giving accommodation for oceangoing vessels at the port of Quebec. We require this amount to continue the work of the present year, which is under contract.
What are these piers like? I understand that one of them toppled over after it was built.

No, the hon. gentleman is misinformed. The work is a very excellent work; the wharfs are built of crib-work under water, and for a certain distance under the water the superstructure is of concrete. We are building a very fine system of piers.
How do these cribworks correspond as to width and height?

They are forty-two feet wide at the base, and sixty-six feet..high, and a good many hundreds of feet in

length, and they are topped off with con-[DOT] erete.
Red liver-improvements at St. Andrew's rapids, $55,000.

The government has been engaged for some time in building a lock and dam at St. Andrew's rapids for the purpose of affording navigation from Lake Winnipeg to the city of Winnipeg. The work is now practically completed, and we expect that in a few days it will be open for navigation.

Does the hon. minister purpose completing the roadway across this superstructure, which I understand is intended to be used as a municipal road? Does he propose making connections with the banks on either side?

What my hon. friend, I suppose, means is, shall we build the approaches so as to enable the people to avail themselves of the bridge, which was built primarily as a service bridge for the lock and dam, as a highway bridge. I may say that we intend to do so.
Then there is no question that the intention of the government is that it shall be a bridge for the use of the public?
There is no question, provided my colleagues agree in the view I take of the matter.

I did not know the government were entering upon a scheme of building municipal bridges. The hon. minister objected very much to spending a few thousand dollars in my county to prevent erosions along the lake shore, insisting that the municipalities should do that. I am not finding fault with the expenditure, but it is rather surprising how conveniently the hon. minister can /accommodate a municipality in one case and refuse a very trifling assistance in another. It is rather remarkable that he should build a municipal bridge in the west and refuse a little consideration in the east.

There is a difference, a very great difference. In this case the character of the river at that point is being changed. The ordinary mode of crossing by boat is necessarily being considerably affected, and I felt that the government, having been obliged to spend a considerable amount of money in building a service bridge for the operation of the lock and lifting curtains, it would not be unreasonable to go a little further and, instead of compelling the municipality to build the approaches, do that work ourselves.

I do not wish the minister to think for a moment that I am Mr. PUGSLEY.
objecting. I think it is a very good idea to provide this service bridge ror the people, because the municipalities contiguous to this portion of the river would certainly be put to a very large expense to erect a bridge. But I am rather amused at the reason the hon. minister has given, that the erection of this dam is going to interfere with the crossing of the river by a ferry. However, I do not wish to make any objection. I think the idea is a very good one.
What will be the increased cost to make the provision for the municipality?
$63,000 is the estimate.
I understand the minister to say that the present vote of $55,000 will complete the opening of the river for all the purposes of navigation, but will not complete the bridge?
This will complete the payments under the existing contracts, but wall not complete the approaches to the bridge or the sodding.
Can the minister give the total cost of the improvements to the rapids, inclusive of the bridge, except the approaches to which he has alluded?
The total expenditure from the beginning will run to about $1,500,000.
What is the tonnage on Lake Winnipeg?

I do not know the tonnage, but there are a considerable number of vessels plying from Selkirk to the foot of the lake. I know that there are two regular steamers and a considerable number of other vessels. It is anticipated that as a result of building these works so as to enable vessels to go right up to the city of Winnipeg the traffic upon the river and lake will be greatly increased in the near future. I have information of at least two vessels which have been constructed especially in view of the construction of this lock and dam. Lake Winnipeg is a very important lake. It is larger than Lake Ontario, and it is impossible to foresee what will be the traffic in the near future.

Before that lock was built one of the objections to it was the danger of ice jamming. The ice used to jam at the mouth of the Red river and raise the water in the city of Winnipeg. I have seen it on the streets there. Has the building of this dam and lock increased to any extent the danger of flooding the city of Winnipeg and district?

We are quite sure that it has not, and the reason of that is that,

owing to the chief engineer of my department having in view the very danger which my hon. friend speaks of, the department engaged upon the construction of a dam and lock which are altogether unique upon the continent. There are some in the old country where the conditions are similar. Here the river takes its rise in the south, the ice melts farther up the river before it does near its mouth, and by a system of lifting or movable curtains we believe we have avoided the possibility of the danger of which my hon. friend speaks.
Mt; J. HAGGART. Is it a movable dam?
Practically a movable dam.
It is taken up on the shore when not in use?
No, it is raised by electrical power.
I have seen them; there is one on the Sault Ste. Marie canal.
No, there is nothing like this in America.
Oh, yes there is.
No.

Pardon me, I have
seen them.
We sent an expert to Europe for the purpose of examining the lock and dam where the conditions are similar, but there is no place in America where there is a similar contrivance.

The dam may be not exactly like the others, but the old dam used for the purpose of stopping the water above the Sault Ste. Marie canal is similar. It is a frame work and they let it into the river with pulleys.
It is altogether different.
And when it is not in use it is lifted up and taken on shore. This is a plan that has been used very often for the purpose of blocking up rivers.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart) has reference to the temporary gates used on the canal in case of accident.
It is for canal purposes.
I have no doubt the foundation principle is the same. But we believe that we have vastly improved upon that by means of this system of lifting curtains.
No doubt.

Perhaps we are not warranted in asking the minister to withhold
the item, but the members for the two constituencies directly interested are not here. My hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. A. Haggart) has not yet returned from his Easter holidays, but I understand that he will 'be here on Saturday. My hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) is in the city, but I have been unable to get in touch ' with him to have him here while this vote is under consideration. I would like if the minister would permit either of these gentlemen at a later stage to speak on the matter.

I would be very glad to. Both of these hon. gentlemen have already spoken on the question, and I am sure that they would regret that there should be any delay in the passing of the item. The hon. member for Selkirk a short time ago spoke in very strong terms of the importance of finishing up these approaches and of the very great importance of the work. But when they come there will be nc objection to their speaking in regard to this when any other item is under discussion, of course, with the permission of the chairman.
St. Jolm harbour, New Brunswick-improvements, $450,000.

This is for the purpose of continuing the work of dredging in the harbour of St. John and of completing the new pier which is now under construction. The work is all under contract, and we anticipate that this amount would be required during the current year.
Will any of this be spent in Courtenay bay?
I am unable to tell my hon. friend at the present time whether it will or not.
Could the minister state whether the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company or the National Transcontinental Railway Commissioners have purchased any land at the head of Courtenay bay?
I may say to my hon. friend that I have been informed that they have agreed to purchase such land, but whether they have actually completed the purchase, I am not aware.
Supposing that the purchase is made, work would have to go on on Courtenay bay, would it not?
I always believe in deciding a matter when the necessity arises.
Then the necessity will not arise this summer?
It does not follow.
The minister has no information to give on the subject?
Not at the present moment.

When the minister is getting a vote, and when an expenditure is to be made at a particular point, he should be prepared to say whether that expenditure is to be made there or not. He should give precise information in reference to what he intends to use the money for.
Suppose he is unable to do so, what then?
Well then, he is not justified in asking for the money.

I may say to my hon. friend that the contracts which are now actually in existence upon the western side of the harbour will require all of this money, provided we keep the dredges upon the western side, but if the Grand Trunk Pacific should complete, as I apprehend they will complete, the purchase of the land around Courtenay bay, then, in the ordinary course, they would, I presume, submit plans for the consideration of the government in regard to the improvements which would be requisite in connection with terminal facilities. Then, it would be my duty to take up the question as to whether we would take some of the dredges that are now employed, upon the western side and place them on Courtenay bay; but at the present moment I cannot decide that because I must know what the Grand Trunk Pacific intend to do before coming to a conclusion.

Does not the minister think that it is perhaps more proper that this expenditure should have the consideration of the House rather than that it should be determined by himself? He has come here proposing an expenditure of money for a purpose; he should give the particular purpose for which the money is to be expended. In answer to my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Daniel), he says that he cannot tell whether a certain amount is to be expended in Courtenay bay or not. That is not an answer. He should have precise information.

I really think that upon reflection my hon. friend will see that I gave a frank statement of what is in my mind at the present time, and that is that the money will be expended upon the western side of the harbour. But, of course, the vote will enable us to expend it on either side of the harbour. If we deemed it necessary in the public interst to expend part on the eastern side of the harbour, I do not see any reason why the government, if they saw fit to do so, could not apply a portion of the money to that purpose, but at the present time it is in contemplation to expend all of this vote upon dredging
and wharf building upon the western side of the harbour.
Can the minister state whether it is the intention of the Grand Trunk Pacific to purchase this land at the head of the bay?
I have been informed that it is the intention of the Grand Trunk Pacific to purchase the land at Courtenay bay, but whether they have actually completed the purchase or not, I am not aware.
The minister has (Stated that (some of this expenditure might be made in Courtenay bay. Have plans and specifications for that part of the work been prepared?	-

Borings have been made in Courtenay bay, and although incomplete they show that a depth of 32 feet of water at low tide can be got without striking rock. Preliminary plans have been prepared by the engineers of my department, although they are not sufficiently matured to enable me to give to the committee any details that would be of value. Before engaging in the work, of course, careful consideration wrnuld be necessary, and detailed plans would have to be worked out.
I presume no contract will be asked for until the detail or working plams are prepared?
None would be entered into.
Is it proposed to do this work by government tenders or to invite tenders for the work that may be decided on after plans have been completed?

Some time ago tenders were called by public advertisement for dredging in St. John harbour, including Courtenay bay. Tenders w'ere received from three contractors: G. S. Mayes, if I remember, asked 74 cents per cubic yard; the Dominion Dredging Company asked 39J cents, and the Maritime Dredging & Contracting Company asked 35 cents per cubic yard, if done with an ordinary dipper dredge, or 25 cents per cubic yard if done with a jsuction or hydraulic dredge. No contract was entered into, but in the contract which wae made for the dredging upon the west side of the harbour it was stipulated that if the government called upon the contractors to do the work of dredging in Courtenay bay they would do it at the price named in their tender. The question as to [DOT]whether it should be done by government dredges or by contract has not been determined. My own view is that there are many advantages in having the work done by a government dredge. I think probably we could get it done more

cheaply even than these low figures named by the contractors, which are much lower than anything which have heretofore been obtained at the port of St. John. When the last contract's were let, under public tender, for the western side of the harbour, the lowest tender was that of G. S. Mayes at 90 cents a cubic yard. In considering whether the work should be done by a government dredge we would have to determine the demands on the government fleet of dredges in other places, and also the question of acquiring additional dredges for the purpose. That matter has not been considered by council and will not be considered until we know whether or not the Grand Trunk Pacific propose to have their terminal at Courtenay bay, which I presume they will do if they complete the purchase of the property, and then the question would come up as to how it would bo best to have the dredging done, whether by contract or by government dredges.

In citing the Maritime Dredging and Contracting Company's tender at 25 cents per cubic yard, the minister omitted to state the qualifying clause, ' provided the material was placed behind revetment walls, etc.'
Mi-. PUGSLEY. That its so.
It is not an ordinary tender?
That is the way in which dredging is done by a suction dredge. You have to do it in that way, you have a long pipe and the material is placed in that way.

From the information I have been able to gather from statements made in the House, tenders were asked for the work at Courtenay bay in 1908. The tenders relating to Courtenay bay were not accepted although the tenderers were under obligation, if called upon, to perform the work which they offered to do, and, as I understand it, the contract was only entered into on behalf of the government with the lowest tenderers for that work on the western side of the harbour.
That is correct.

The minister states that no complete detail or working plans have been prepared and the extent of the work has not been determined by the department for the proposed expenditure. I have been led to believe that the dredging alone would cost two or three millions. I may be wrong, but I gathered from an answer in the House some weeks ago that when these tenders were invited only $6,000 of a deposit was required. Evidently the government did not contemplate so great an expenditure on the part of the contractors when they only askec} the contractors to furnish a deposit of $6,000. Of course if the government only propose to carry out the contract, and not have any work done in Courtenay bay by these contractors, that would seem to be all right. But if it is proposed to extend that work, then I do not think it is in the public interest to take a step involving so large an expenditure without inviting tenders for the work which has yet to be determined. Now, the minister has stated that this vote is for the western side, and that possibly in consequence of some contingent action on the part of the Grand Trunk Pacific it might be necessary to have the dredges on the western side of the harbour removed to Courtenay bay to do that work. Then it must be in the mind of the minister that the contractors tor the western side of the harbour propose to do the work on the Courtenay bay side. I simply want to know whether that is in contemplation and if it is involved in this vote, because if it is, I would take serious exception to it, and would take the trouble to advance reasons why that should not be done. I simply ask the minister that I may know, and that the country may know, his plans in respect to the matter.

I notice that the minister says he has, not yet decided whether the work to be done in St. John harbour shall be done by contract or by government dredges. A year ago I asked for a return of the number of dredges owned by the government, and the work they had heen doing during the last three years. The return shows the amount of work these dredges have done, and I have made up a statement of the relative cost of doing the work which has been done by government dredges, and the cost of work done by similar dredges which are owned by contractors ; and I intend on another occasion to speak at greater length on this matter. But I wish to call the attention of the minister to the fact that wore can be done, and is being done, by contractors at a cheaper price than the work that is being done by government dredges. The government owns at present an enormous fleet of dredges and dredging plant, I think they own a greater amount of dredging plant than they should own. I am absolutely opposed to doing work of that kind by government dredges. If the hon. minister will look at the work which was done by the dredge 'W. S. Fielding' in St. John harbour during 12 months, he will find that the work done by that dredge, apparently working continuously for the 12 months, did not exceed the amount which such a dredge should do in two months. The dredge cost over_ $600,000, and working foT 12 months straightaway, winter and summer, it moved less than 400,000 yards of material. A dredge which cost that

much money ought to remove that much material in two months.
What kind of material?

Ordinary clay; this dredge would not work in any other kind of material, it would not work in harder material. It is an endless bucket dredge, and works only in. comparatively soft material, it would not work in hard pan.
That is just what it is doing in St. John harbour, the very hardest kind of material.

I won't dispute the hon. gentleman, because he apparently lives there. But my knowledge of such dredges is that they usually work in comparatively soft material, not in what is called hard-pan and boulders, because the buckets are not large enough to hold large boulders. I am positive that if the minister looks over the Tecords he will find that the government own at present all the dredges that they should own, and that the policy of the government in buying and building more dredges should be reversed, that work of this kind should be let by public tender, that it should be let to the lowest bidder, that there should be no arrangements made with bidders beforehand, but the man who is the lowest bidder on that particular job should get the work.

I am glad to hear what my hon. friend (Mr. German) has just said. I quite agree with him when he says that when contracts are let they should be given to the lowest bidder. But I may say to my hon. friend, and I am sure he will agree with me from his knowledge of what has taken place, that that is the case in all contracts let by the Department of Public Works, and I believe by all other departments of the government. But the question which my hon. friend raises as to whether it is better to do dredging by government dredges or by contract, is one with regard to which there may very properly be differences of opinion. My own view, notwithstanding what my hon. friend has said, is strongly that it is in the public interest to extend the number of government-owned dredges. I would like myself to see all the dredging of the country performed by government dredges. While, perhaps, there may not be just as much work done by government dredges per day as may be done by contract dredges, yet upon the whole, I think they can do the work more cheaply, because contractors, of course, necessarily figure upon the cost of their plant, they naturally look for reasonable profits from their work, and of course each contractor has to insure for himself. So, upon the whole I am Mr. GERMAN.
inclined to think that it would be to the public advantage to increase the number of government dredges rather than diminish it. But, of course, that is a matter of opinion with regard to which hon. gentlemen may differ. Now a word with regard to the dredge ' Fielding.' My hon. friend makes a comparison of its work with work which may be done by a contract dredge in some other section of the country. You cannot make a reliable comparison in that way. The dredge ' Fielding ' is dredging the channel of the harbour of St. John. The material consists of hard material, in addition there are a good many boulders. I have been on board the dredge, and I have seen the operations stopped by very large boulders getting into the buckets, and when one of these boulders does get in the buckets it delays the operation of the dredge for a considerable time. It is dredging out a part of the harbour where it is greatly exposed to the weather, as gales arise there frequently, and when these storms occur the dredge has to stop working To make a proper comparison one Would have to take a contract for dredging at a similar place, and under similar circumstances. It is to be borne in mind that the dredge ' Fielding ' is dredging to a depth of 55-feet below the water when the tide is high, and there is a wonderful difference between working under those circumstances and going into a bank of soft mud, and simply shovelling out the soft material by means of a dipper. I took pains to make inquiries as to the work being done by the ' Fielding ' last summer, and while I cannot give the exact figures, I believe it was doing most creditable work.
In July, 1909, it dug out 69,000 cubic yards, and in August 52,400.
Under the circumstances it was doing very good work. With ordinary dredging material, 10,000 cubic yards per day is an unusual quantity.
What kind of a dredge?
An elevator dredge with an endless chain of buckets.
What is the capacity of the buckets?

About one cubic yard, taking about one ton to each bucket." In reply to the question of my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson), I do not think that the dredging in Courtenay bay is involved in this vote, because if we should contemplate dredging at that bay, we would have to get a larger vote. Should we come to the conclusion to do that work, we would have necessarily to ask for an additional amount in the supplementaries, and my hon. friends would then have the opportunity of fully discussing the item.
When introducing this vote, the hon. gentleman said that a portion of it might be used for dredging at Courtenay bay.

But involved in that was the understanding that I would have to obtain a further vote in the supplemen-taries. But if there be no further vote, I would not use any part of this in that work because the vote would be too small.

The hon. minister went further. He asked for tenders, and awarded a contract, and those tenders covered that particular work of dredging out Courtenay bay, and he did that without a vote from parliament at all.

No.
Mr 1. HAGGART. We knew nothing about Courtenay bay until the hon. member for Westmorland gave the information.
The information I gave was contained in a return made before the House.

Then I am only speaking for myself. I did not know the information until I heard it given by the hon. member for Westmorland. To my astonishment I hear that this, involves an expenditure of between two and.three million dollars for dredging Courtenay bay. The plans and specifications, and an estimate of the cost, and a full statement of the work to be done should be given by the minister before he asks for a dollar. The minister corrects himself now, and says he would not venture upon the work without a subsequent vote. That was not the statement he made on the introduction of the vote. According to that statement, it appeared that we were giving the minister power to make an expenditure in Courtenay bay. I protest against any such manner of introducing so important a vote -a vote that will add to the enormous expenditure which we are at present making on the Transcontinental an expenditure of over $3,000,000. We should have the plans and specifications, and a complete estimate. What authority had the minister to ask for tenders for the purpose of beginning the work?
We had a vote in 1908 of $400,000 for St. John harbour.
That does not include Courtenay bay.
Yes it does.

The vote for St. John harbour, we are now told, covers the expenditure on another place which is a little distant from that harbour-a new harbour proposed for the use of the Grand Trunk Pacific That was never explained, and
we would not have known anything about Courtenay bay only we saw in the newspapers that the Grand Trunk Pacific intended to purchase it for a terminus. What this House must have is a statement showing what work is contemplated, and the necessity for it, and a complete estimate of the expenditure. If the statement of the hon. member for Westmorland is correct, the expenditure involved is between two and three million dollars. ,

I want to correct an error into which my hon, friend evidently has fallen, and perhaps not unnaturally, because he says this is the first time he heard of any proposed improvements at Courtenay bay. The reason is he was not aware of the return having been brought down, to which my hon. friend from Westmorland has referred. He says that we entered into a contract for the dredging of Courtenay bay. That is what we did not do.
The hon. gentleman received tenders for the purpose of doing this work?

Yes, but in my judgment Courtenay bay is a part of St. John harbour. Vessels have been for a hundred years going up Courtenay bay. There are one or two small wharfs at the head of the bay, and vessels have always gone there. By the charter of the city, that bay is declared to be a part of the city and harbour of St. John. True, the boundary is at Marsh creek, which runs down through the bay, but it is a part of the harbour. I did call for tenders, but we did not enter into any contract. The matter, therefore, is in this position, that if the government should decide to go on with the work of assisting in the terminals of the Grand Trunk Pacific, should the Grand Trunk Pacific decide to make a terminal there, if, will be open to the government to determine whether that work should be done by contract or by one or more government dredges. My hon. friend misunderstood me when he understood me to say that a part of this money would be used for dredging at Courtenay bay. The hon. member for the city of St. John (Mr. Daniel) asked me if a part would be so used, and I said I did not know. The reason I do not know is because I cannot tell whether the government will decide to put in the supplementary estimates any amount for the purpose of dredging out that bay. But I can assure the committee that unless there should be a further amount voted for dredging out Courtenay bay, no part of this vote will be used for that purpose. But if there should be an amount in the supplementaries, the matter can be fully discussed, and plans will be submitted. In making this statement, I want it to be clearly understood that the government has not decided to do

any dredging at Courtenay bay. The matter is entirely open. I am only speaking now of what may take place in case an amount should be put in the supplementary estimates. Personally, I am in favour of proceeding at an early date to make improvements at Courtenay bay, always provided that the Grand Trunk decide upon that as their terminal. That is only my own individual view; the government has not considered the matter at all. If it should be decided to go on, it would necessarily come in further estimates, and then the matter wouy be all open for discussion.

The statement made by the minister is as I would have expected. Knowing from the return, the circumstances connected with it, I did not for a moment assume that this vote was intended for the development of that portion of the harbour of St. John known as Courtenay Bay harbour. I recognized that tenders had been asked for dredging in St. John harbour, inclusive of Courtenay bay, but I also recognized that the government had not entered into any such contract, and that in making the contract with the successful tenderers they provided in it that they could call upon the contractors to do work in Courtenay bay if they desired, but that the contractors could not hold the government under any obligation to give them the work or to have the work done. I, therefore, assumed that there would be no such work entered upon by these contractors, and furthermore, I had assumed that if any work was entered upon, we would have the full plans and specifications laid before parliament, and that tenders would be asked for that additional work. In a work that involves millions of dolllars, you would naturally expect that those who would be invited to compete for it should make a greater deposit than a mere pittance of $6,000; a pittance in comparison to the great expenditure. As I understand the minister, the matter stands in this way: that no part of this sum of $450,000 is to be expended in connection with the Courtenay bay work.
Unless there should be a further sum asked for.
Then you would have the two amounts aggregated?
Yes.

I want to impress as emphatically as I can on the minister my views as to the policy of the government owning and operating government dredges. I may say that the ' Fielding ' -and this applies to almost every dredge that is operated by the government-the 'Fielding' cost $612,784; she worked the whole year from the 1st of April, 1908, to the 1st of March, 1909, and she excavated Mr. PUGSLEY.
only 350,540 cubic yards, and J am in the judgment of the engineer of the department, that that dredge should have done that amount of work in two months. An ordinary dipper dredge which will not cost more than $30,000 will excavate 5,000 cubic yards of material in a day.
Oh, no.
I know whereof I speak.
How much did the ' Fielding ' cost?
She cost $612,784; the cost of operating her for twelve months was $61,221, and the cost of maintaining her for the twelve months $14,113.
How much did she earn?
I would not think she would be earning anything.
What was the value of the work she did?

Taking operating and maintenance expenses, and without calculating anything for interest or for depreciation, the cost would amount to about twenty-two cents per yard. What applies to the ' Fielding ' applies to every dredge owned by the government, as I believe I can emphatically show the minister. The dredging done by the government dredges costs more than the dredging done by contract work.
A dipper dredge could not operate at all where the * Fielding ' has been operating, because she is exposed to the winds and the roll of the Bay of Fundy.
I am not saying anything about that, but let her do more work for the money that is being spent on her.

I know myself of dredges owned by contractors which have cost from $100,000 to $150,000 and more, and in fifty feet of water upon the sea-coast they never make on an average more than from 1,000 to 1,500 cubic yards a day. There is not a dipper dredge in Canada that in fifty feet of water could dredge 5,000 cubic yards a day. My hon. friend (Mr. German) would want to pursue the inquiry further, and consider what is done by contract dredges working under similar conditions to the ' Fielding '. We are getting dredging done by contract as low as eleven cents in some places, while in other places we are paying ninety cents per cubic yard. Some dredges do work as low as one and a half cents per cubic yard, and others do it at twenty cents, forty cents, sixty cents; it all depends upon the conditions. The splendid hydraulic dredge ' J. I. Tarte ', does work at three or four cents per cubic yard under peculiarly advantageous circumstances.
What does dredging cost per cubic yard on the Red river?
I have not that information at hand.
What is the estimated total amount to be spent on St. John harbour, including Courtenay bay?

It depends entirely upon the extent of the work to be done, and of course that depends upon the development of the business. The development of St. John as a winter port began in 1895, and since then the business has been increasing from year to year until now it has reached a volume of from twenty millions to twenty-five million dollars of exports during the winter season. The number of steamers coming to that harbour is constantly increasing, and we hope the number will continue to increase. It will take many, many years before the St. John harbour will be finally completed. What it will eventually cost I am unable to say. At present we are building a wharf upon the western side of the harbour which will accommodate two additional steamers; we are doing dredging for a series of wharfs which will be needed in the future, and we are making provision for the building of an additional wharf in the near future which will give accommodation for two more steamers. When we have done that, I think we might let the work rest for a few years, until the trade develops still further, and there is a more urgent demand for additional wharfs.
Can the minister give the total expenditure bv his department and by the Railway Department on the harbour of St. John from 1867 to the present time?
I am sorry to say that I have not that information.

Has the minister received any serious complaints from Port Arthur to the effect that some of the contractors who were dredging there and who had orders to carry out the material in the night-time frequently went out with only a few barrow fulls, and that the inspectors were not doing their duty in that district?
No such complaint has reached me.
Will the minister look into the matter?
If my hon. friend will be good enough to furnish me with any details he has in his possession, I shall be very glad to look into it.
I have reason to believe that it is worth the minister's while to look into the matter-to ask his inspectors at least.
It is last year that my hon. friend refers to?
Yes.
If my hon. friend has any further information and will give it to me, I shall be glad to have the matter investigated.
Do these improvements relate solely to dredging or do they include other matters?
They include dredging and the building of a wharf now under construction on the western side of the harbour. *
Not on Courtenay bay?
No.
How far is Courtenay bay from that wharf?
The entrance to Courtenay bay is less than half a mile. It begins just at the eastern side of what is ordinarily known as the harbour of St. John.
The minister obviously has some plan of improvement in contemplation when he is asking for this vote. The question was put to him a little while ago, and he did not answer it.

Yes, I have a complete plan of contemplated improvements on the west side, which it is hoped the business of the future will require-not the immediate future, but we must look forward a good many years in the case of a port which is rapidly developing. This plan includes dredging from Sand point to the Beacon bar, and a series of ships berths between these two points. When the development is finally completed, it will give additional accommodation for about ten ocean steamers.
Is this below the Canadian Pacifiol terminals?
Yes, to the southward.
How many berths are there now?

I think there is accommodation for six ocean steamers, and we are at present providing for two more. The plan contemplates ten in addition to these two, giving accommodation for about 18 steamers in all.
I also understood from the minister that he desires authority to devote a portion of this vote to development in Courtenay bay?

No, we would require the greater part of this amount to complete the wharfs which are now under construe-

tion on the west side and in order to finish up the dredging work lor the additional wharf we contemplate building to the south of Sand point; and therefore, unless we had a further vote, it would be useless to take any part of this for the development of Courtenay bay. No part of this will be devoted to that purpose. If we should ask for a further amount, then I will bring such plans as we have, and give the committee all necessary information in regard to it.

I simply wanted a clear understanding of the matter. If any portion of this money is to be devoted to improvements at Courtenay bay, then the country would, of course, be committed to some plan of development there, in which case we would want the minister's explanation. But I understand that no portion of this money will be devoted to the carrying out of any plan at Courtenay bay until a further sum is asked for and full explanations of such plan are given to the committee.
Quite so.
Has the land at Courtenay bay been acquired by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company?

I have been informed by the company that they had made an arrangement to purchase the land at Courtenay bay,, this will take in all the land at the head of the bay and also the foreshore right of Messrs. Gilbert, the owners of the property.
How large an area?

The land at the head of the bay covers an area of about 75 acres, and the tide flats cover several hundred acres, of which they would be the riparian owners. Whether they have actually completed. the purchase or not I have not been informed.

I saw it stated in the press, regarding the option said to be held for this purpose, that the area on the shore was 31 or 32 acres and that there was a similar area of foreshore about 64 or 65 acres altogether.
I think my hon. friend has been misinformed as to that. I thjnk it takes in all the head of Courtenay bay, extending from the Marsh creek around to the property owned by the late Mr. Dunn.
The minister is not in a position_ to state whether the Grand Trunk Pacific intend to buy that additional area or not?

All I can say to my hon. friend is that the officials of the company have informed me that they have decided to purchase the property, but whether they Mr. PUGSLEY
have completed the purchase or not I am unable to say.

Could not facilities be provided for the accommodation of the Grand Trunk Pacific on the west side of the harbour? If so, it would save a very large expenditure which will otherwise have to be undertaken by this country in connection with the Courtenay bay project.

The company have, through their officials, informed me, that they have their engineer at St. John and they are of opinion that the west side would not, owing to the difficulty of the approach, afford to them the adequate facilities that they want for their terminal. As my hon. friend is no doubt aware, in order to get to the west side they would have to use the Canadian Pacific railway, crossing over by their line at the falls and then going around to the terminals of the Canadian Pacific railway. Rival companies have (serious objections to using each other's lines, I suppose, because of the difficulty of making arrangements. But the president of the Grand Trunk Pacific, Mr. Hays, has informed me that Courtenay bay presents an ideal site for terminals, and he has also told me that ajs a result of a visit to St. John of their engineer, he is of opinion that this presents the only opportunity at St. John which would enable them to get the terminals which they would desire for the great business they expect will go over the Transcontinental railway. They could get limited accommodation in connection with the Intercolonial terminals, but their opinion is that Courtenay bay nresents the ideal opportunity for railway terminals.
How many berths are there at the Intercolonial railway terminals?
Only two, and they are filled all the time during the winter with the present business.
Are they capable of extension?
Other property might be bought at the head of the harbour, but the difficulty i's to get yard room. Space is very limited at the head of the harbour, as my hon. friend from St. John knows.

I understand that the wharfs that the minister mentioned in connection with the harbour at St. John are wharfs which are provided for the moving of commerce generally. How much wharfage has the minister there?

Of course, there are wharfs in connection with the Intercolonial railway. The Intercolonial has two berths for ocean steamers at the head of the harbour, and then there is also what is known as the ballast wharf terminal. That makes

three. But at the ballast wharf I do not think the water is deep enough for the largest ocean steamers. Upon the western side of the harbour the wharfs have practically all, up to the present time, betejn. constructed by the city of St. John.
By private individuals?

No, by the corporation of St. John at their own expense, and the people have felt that a heavy burden has been imposed on them because they have been called upon to provide terminal facilities for the trade of Canada, not for the local trade, but to enable the exports and imports of Canada in the winter season to pass through a Canadian port. They have expended in the vicinity of $1,250,000 for that purpose. It has been expended for a national purpose, and they have not felt that they could go any further. They came to me when I was elected and became minister and urged that further facilities ought to be provided at the expense of Canada, keeping in mind all they had done for this national purpose. I then, with the approval of my colleagues, entered upon the construction of a wharf in extension of the wharfs which had been built by the city upon the western side of the harbour, and the department is now building an additional wharf which will give accommodation for two more ocean steamers on the western side. Then, we have in contemplation, in the near future, the building of another wharf to the south of Sand point which will give accommodation for two more steamers.
There are no privately owned docks?

Not for ocean steamers.
Tiffin harbour-improvements, $120,000.

This is to continue the work of drilling and dredging at Tiffin. We are providing for a depth of 25 feet at low water. This i<s to provide a harbour in connection with the Grand Trunk railway. I may say this is a part of the national transportation scheme which was recommended by the Transportation Commission whose recommendations the government is endeavouring to carry out. Tiffin harbour ifs to be used pimarily as a point for the transhipment of the products of the west. The Grand Trunk railway are building a railway with a grade not exceeding four-tenths of one per cent eastward, over which they will be able to carry large trains of cars with one locomotive, and they hope so to reduce the cost-and in this they are emulating the Canadian Pacific railway in connection with their work at Victoria harbour-of carrying grain eastward that they will be able to divert a large portion of the grain froth the Northwest which now goes by way of Buffalo and 195
other American ports through Canadian channels and Canadian seaports. This is a very important national work, and we are asking for this amount in order to carry it to completion. We hope that by next fall we will be able to give deep water accommodation up to the splendid system of elevators which the Grand Trunk are building at Tiffin.
The Grand Trunk have heretofore been using Midland. Do they intend to establish a new port at Tiffin?
Yes, their through transportation business will be done at Tiffin.
I would like to ask the minister if these wharfs being built at Tiffin are on property owned by the government or by the Grand Trunk?
The government is not building any wharfs at Tiffin. All the wharf building is being done by the Grand Trunk itself.
Has the government built none of the wharfs in the past there?
No.
Is this intended to complete this dredging or only a part of it?
It ought to very nearly complete the work we have in hand there.
What is the railway company spending there?
Several million dollars. They are building a magnificent elevator and wharfs, they are sipending a large amount.
Is this by contract?

Yes, by contract let after public tender to the Canadian Dredging and Construction Company at twenty-nine cents per cubic yard for ordinary material.
Vancouver harbour, British Columbia-improvements, $67,500.

I explained this the other day. We are asked to make very considerable improvements at Vancouver. One is the widening of the First Narrows. The entrance to the harbour is only about 600 feet wide. There is quite a heavy run of tide, and often it is foggy, and by reason of the great increase in the number of vessels entering the harbour there is considerable danger attending the navigation of that part of it. Some time ago a collision occurred, and some lives were lost. We propose widening the harbour to 1,200 feet. There are also some improvements at the entrance of False creek which we have under consideration.



Victoria harbour, British Columbia-improvements, $48,750.

This is a very important work. It will consist of rock drilling, and dredging in Victoria harbour to improve the channel, and also broadening out the inner harbour in the vicinity of the Canadian Pacific Bailway dock, and the new dock about to be constructed by the Grand Trunk Pacific. My information is that the business of Victoria is rapidly increasing. During the present season there will be a considerable addition to the number of steamers frequenting the port, and the improvement seems necessary to accommodate the increased shipping. We propose acquiring, if our information as to their usefulness is confirmed, two Lob-nitz rock breakers to carry on the work of rock-drilling as rapidly as possible, and we will have one or more dredges to remove the rock as it is broken. We propose continuing as rapidly as we can the general work of improving the harbour.
I understood from the minister that this would not be sufficient for the purchase of these machines.

The question of what additional amount should be voted is now before council.
Victoria harbour, Ontario-improvements, $108,750.

This represents to the Canadian Pacific railway what Tiffin represents to the Grand Trunk railway. It is a part of the transportation system of the Canadian Pacific. railway. They are building elevators, and wharfs, and the government is doing the dredging. I think this will nearly if not entirely complete the work we have in hand at Victoria harbour. It is under contract to the Canadian Dredging and Construction Company at 12J cents for ordinary material, and $2.25 for rock and boulders. That illustrates -the difference in cost. There you have the ordinary material tendered for by the lowest tenderer at 12J cents at Victoria, Ontario, and 29 cents at Tiffin more than twice as much at Tiffin as at Victoria harbour, and yet the contracts in both cases were let after wide public competition, and to the lowest tenderer.
The same class of dredge?

The same class of dredge. It is the difference in the conditions, and the material to be dredged. In one case the contractors thought it would be worth 29 cents, and they tendered at that. In the other case it was 124 cents.

It is to be hoped they will not be able to count up the material as the contractors have been able to do on the Grand Trunk Pacific or they should Mr. PUGSLEY.
make a very profitable thing on it. I suppose the government can only depend on their inspector to ascertain the different quantities of the different materials?

We have taken every precaution to protect the public interest. I recognized after I became minister the fact that the country was to a certain extent at the mercy of the inspectors, and I have taken every precaution to guard against any. improper iconduct on their part. We require them not only to prepare returns as to the quantities, but to make a solemn declaration, which is the same as an oath, that they are on the work, that they personally inspect each scow load that goes out, and make the measurement in the manner prescribed. We also inspect the inspectors, we have persons who are inspecting them, and their work as well.
Is that a new office, an inspector of inspectors?
No, it is not a new office.
Is it a new policy?
We do that through the resident engineers, and their assistants. We keep careful oversight over the inspectors.

Before that item is passed, I would like to call the attention of the minister to the fact that there is no fish-way provided at St. Andrew's rapids, and the river is in a very unsatisfactory condition so far as fishing is concerned. It was a serious oversight not to provide a fish-way. I drew the attention of the Marine Department some time ago to the fact, and I understood they were to take it up with the minister. Has that been done?
The matter has not yet been brought to my attention by the Marine Department, but I will have it looked into.

I would like to impress upon the minister the importance of this matter, because under present conditions no fish from Lake Winnipeg can get past the St. Andrew's dam; consequently the upper part of my constituency and the city of Winnipeg are denied the use of those fish.
Would the fish venture past the sewers of the city of Winnipeg, and would that affect them at all?

Not at all.
Dredging in Quebec and Ontario, $675,000.

This amount is to make provision for operating during the present yeaT the dredging plant, and also to make payments for work which will be done under contract in different places. In the

province of Quebec work will be done at various points on the lakes and rivers, also in the province of Ontario a good deal of work will be done at various harbours upon Lakes Ontario, Erie, Huron and the Georgian bay.
How about Port Credit?
I think that is a private harbour, is it not?
Sometimes my hon. friend expends public money on private harbours.

I would ask the minister what new dredging plant he proposes to acquire in the province of Ontario? I see that he has a vote for new dredging plant in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, as well as other provinces. If it is a proper question, I would like to know what dredging plant the department intends to acquire in Ontario?

We require to get a hull for the dredge ' Nipissing,' a new boiler and machinery for the dredge ' Nipissing,' a new boiler and machinery for the ' Sir John,' a new hull for the ' Challenge,' a new boiler for the ' Mattawa.' two new 32-cubic yard dump scows for the ' Deschenes,' six yawl boats for different vessels, a new light draft tug for dredge No. 3, dippers for several dredges, costing about $500, a new engine for the ' Storm King,' new steel spuds for the ' Industry,' a steel scow and new spuds for the ' International.' We want to do some work upon the tugs ' Lisgar ' and ' Peel,' and to complete some payments, amounting to $4,200. The total is $135,000.
Boes the minister propose to purchase any dredging plant in the province of Ontario the coming season?
Not out of this vote.

I understood the minister proposed to purchase some dredging plant from the Dominion Dredging Company. I must say, as I have already said, that I think the government has got all the dredging plant they require, and why they should purchase dredging plant from a company which is now in the dredging business and building new dredges, I cannot understand.
There were some negotiations, but no decision has been arrived at.
Is it the intention of the government to operate the dredge now at Lake Nipissing?
Yes.

This dredge did certain work at the mouth of the South river last year, but on account of the removal of the roller dam at the foot of Lake Nipissing, 195J
this work has become of little or no use at the present time. The level of the lake has been so much lowered by the removal of these dams that the dredging is of little use. I think some improvement should be made there.
Mr, PUGSLEY. The improvement of conditions on Lake Nipissing is engaging the earnest attention of the department. We are confronted with the difficulty that if we maintain dams at the outlet of the lake, the country is liable to be flooded, and if we do not maintain the necessary dams then the water becomes too low for vessels in many cases to navigate the lake. We are giving earnest attention to the question, and hope we will be able to improve conditions there.
I think the minister will find that the trouble at Lake Nipissing is largely caused by the unusual way the dams were built. They were entirely useless in the way they were built.
If we should decide to build new ones, we will endeavour to avoid any mistakes that may have been made,

I wish to take the occasion of this item to direct the minister's attention to a promise that was made by the government some years ago, and repeated year after year by the Minister of Public Works, that some dredging would be done at Port Credit, Lake Ontario. It is rather an important point, lying between the city of Toronto and the city of Hamilton, on Lake Ontario, where there is a good deal of traffic in the summer time. It was also looked upon as a harbour of refuge. My hon. friend in past years has stated that it was a private harbour. It is a private harbour, but I think it would be in the public interest, and that the government would be discharging a public duty, if they made an appropriation, or took some portion of this money, to do some dredging in that harbour. Many years ago the government did dredge the harbour out and made some pretty liberal expenditure on that work. At that time it was a private harbour and there has been no change since, except that it may have passed from one private owner to another. My hon. friend always in committee, when I have drawn his attention to this matter, has replied that the government cannot spend money on private harbours. But I would like to point out that his department and his predecessors, have spent public money on private harbours. I am not saying that the policy is a good or a bad one, but there are exceptional cases, and this is a case in which there is a great deal of traffic interested. There is a lighthouse in that harbour which is kept up by the government, and a great deal of shipping is going on there at present. A considerable amount of products of

different kinds are taken in and out of it, but they can only be taken by very small boats, because of the condition of the harbour, owing to the fact that there has been no dredging done there for many years. I want, as emphatically as I can, to draw my hon. friend's attention to it, and ask if he will not allow some engineer of his department to inspect and make a report upon it, so that he may see whether it would be a wise and proper expenditure to apply some of this money to the dredging of that harbour.
Is Port Credit in my hon. friend's constituency?
Yes.
I understood my hon. friend to say that he would not say whether it was a wise or an unwise policy to expend public money on dredging in a private harbour, yet he urges me to do it in this case.

I think it would be a very wise expenditure, and my hon. friend's supporters think it would be also. My hon. friend has in his department at this moment more than one very largely signed petition, signed by the ratepayers in that section, calling on the government to make this expenditure. I said I did not know whether it was wise or unwise to make it a policy of the government to spend public money on private harbours, but that there were exceptional cases, and I regarded this as an exceptional one. It is a very important point; there is a great deal of traffic between Toronto and Hamilton, and this is looked upon as a natural harbour of refuge. A very small expenditure indeed would protect what has already been expended by a former government in that harbour; but if the harbour be allowed to continue in its present condition, and the condition is getting worse and worse every year, it will become useless. If the government does not very soon make some expenditure of public money there it will be necessary to spend a very large amount. My hon. friend will understand my answer to his question when I say that I have no hesitation in declaring that this would be a very wise expenditure. If, when in Toronto, he would take a run out there and see it himself, or if he would send an engineer to examine it, he would find that I am not putting the case at all too strongly.

As the matter has a good deal of importance, not merely to Port Credit, but also to other harbours which are similarly situated, I desire to say that I am rather surprised that my hon. friend who is declaring generally that he is not able to state whether it is a wise or unwise course for the government to Mr. BLAIN.
spend money on private harbours, but that, in respect of this particular harbour, which happens to be in his constituency, and for reasons which no doubt are eminently satisfactory to himself, the expenditure would be a wise one.
I did not say that this was the only case.

Of course, it is always easy to make exceptional cases and ask for expenditure for exceptional reasons. I am rather of the opinion that it would be very much better if the people living at Port Credit and at other places where there are private harbours, which their owners are not able to keep in repair, would induce these proprietors to part with the ownership of these horbours and hand them over to the government. I have never been able to understand the policy which induced past governments to hand over the control of harbours to private companies. If there be anything which ought to be owned by the public it is a harbour. I would suggest to my hon. friend whether it would not be better for the people to try and induce this company, which apparently is not able to' keep this harbour in proper condition, to hand it over to the Crown, and then I would be pleased to give the matter my most favourable consideration. But even although it is a private harbour, I will not say that I will not make the improvements. I shall have the matter looked into, and if I feel that the work can be done at a reasonable cost, and I can justify it to my colleagues and to this House, I will give it my favourable consideration.

I know something about Port Credit harbour, and under existing conditions I think it would be an exceedingly unwise policy for the government to spend any money on its improvements. It is very currently rumoured, whether the rumour be true or untrue, that this harbour was purchased simply with the view of getting the government to spend money on it and make it more valuable, and then handing it over to the government at the enhanced value caused by this government expenditure.
Can the hon. gentleman give any reasons for that statement?
I say there is a rumour to that effect, whether true or untrue.
Who are the owners that are seeking to do this?
My hon. friend must know who thS owners are.-
I thought the hon. gentleman did not know much about it.

I do not know who the owners are, but I have an idea, however.

There is another point I wish to bring to the attention of the minister with regard to the dredging of harbours, l think that in that connection the government could change their policy to the public advantage. I refer to the manner of letting contracts for dredging work in the various harbours on the lakes on which the province of Ontario borders. The policy of the government is to let contracts each spring for work to he done during the season of navigation, and I would suggest to the minister that a better way would be, in the first place, to ascertain the amount of dredging required to be done in each harbour especially, and then call for tenders for the whole work. Let the whole job to the lowest tenderer, and then he would know that when he got his plant on the work it would remain there until the work was completed. The minister will certainly get a lower price for the work under these conditions than if he only lets it for one season, because the contractor may be obliged the following season to move his plant on to some other piece of work, and to tow it there under very large expenditure and risk. I have heard it said that one reason why the government thinks it necessary to own a dredging plant is to prevent a combine amongst the contractors. But if at Port Hope, or Hamilton, or Cobourg, or Midland, or at Victoria,, the dredging work to be done on these lake harbours was let to the contractor, not for one season, but for two seasons or five seasons until it was completed, then you would have actual competition among the dredge-men, because the fact that their plant would Temain there until the work was completed would be an incentive to them to get down to the lowest possible price. If the minister considers this matter with the officers of his department, I believe he will find that it will tend to the saving of money and the doing of the work more . expeditiously than under the present system.	*

I entirely agree with the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. German) and I may tell him that the department has adopted that policy and the advertisements now published do not limit the dredging to one season.
That was the system in the past.

Yes, in most cases, but now we estimate as nearly as we can what quantity of dredging the government is prepared to do in the public interest at these different places, and we call for tenders for the whole work whether it takes one year or two years. I have a remarkable instance of the truth of what my hon. friend (Mr. German) has said in the case of the dredging at St. John harbour,
where, before I became minister the work was let for one season, and 90 cents a yard was the lowest tender, but when I became minister it was given to be understood that the contract would not be limited to the one season and the result was that a tender was received tc do the work which would run over a number of years, at 39i cents per cubic yard, or a little over one-third of what had been previously paid when the contract was let for onlv one year. I believe the adoption of this policy will result in great saving to the country and I shall adopt it as far as I reasonably can.

I was surprised to hear the hon. member (Mr. German) suggest to the government that it would be unwise to make any expenditure in the harbour of Port Credit, because, as he said, there was a rumour that some company owned this harbour and was desirous of getting public money expended upon it, with the view, I would take it, of making money. Did I understand the hon. gentleman correctly?
You did.

If that be the case it will be all in his own family and it has nothing to do with any members on this side of the House. However, I think it is rather a vague rumour. I never heard of such a thing in the county in which the harbour is situated, and I do not think that any person else who lives there ever heard of such a thing being suggested. There is only one reason for expenditure in the harbour of Port Credit and that reason is the public weal. If my hon. friend from Welland will look over the harbour I think he will revise his statement and that he will come back here and suggest that money should be expended on that harbour, no matter what dredging company gets the contract. At all events, the government has a precedent because in years gone by public money was expended there.
Is this money to be expended for paying the government dredges or for the letting of contracts?
Both.

The more business-like plan would be for the government to ascertain how much was to be exnended in each harbour and then submit an estimate to parliament for the expenditure at each place. The present system leaves a great deal of discretion with the government and they can use this money in almost any way they like. It is sometimes uncharitably said that they occasionally use this money for the betterment of their own friends rather than for the betterment of the harbour. I am not saying whether that is so or not, but as the hon. gentleman from Welland (Mr. German) says it is one of the rumours. I know that there ars

instances when, because of urgency, dred-; ging has to be done at a particular place, but in voting these large sums of money for general purposes I do not think we are following a sound princiole.

I would like to be permitted at this juncture to supplement the information which I gave to the minister a few days ago with respect to some dredging which is needed in Western Nova Scotia. I may say, with regard to the port of Weymouth, to which I drew the minister's attention at that time, that I have since been informed by some people who are interested in the shipping business there, that there were originally two channels into that harbour, and that during the time the Hon. Mr. Vail occupied a seat in this House-then I think the Minister of Militia and Defence, and representative of the county of Digby-he had one of those channels dammed up with stone with the view of having the other one opened out by dredging. His idea was that a greater flow of water would pass through the wider channel by reason of the closing of the other one. His anticipation in this was not fulfilled, however, and thereafter no dredging was done there, so that what was a fairly tolerable channel at one time has been blocked up, and no other channel has been substituted for it. The old channel gave twelve feet of water at low tide. The present channel does not give anything like that depth, and a small amount of dredging at the bar, as a beginning would make a very great improvement. I merely submit this for the information of the minister, because he was good enough to say the other evening that the matter would have his careful consideration. Now just a word as to the work that ha3 been done at Weymouth heretofore, and as to the revenues which that port has turned into the public treasury. I am informed by people living in that town, who tell me that they are well assured of the accuracy of their statements, that with the exception of this damming of that one channel, no public money has been expended on improvements there since confederation. They further tell me that between $300,000 and $400,000 has been paid into the public treasury in the way of customs duties collected at that port, and they ask in all fairness that a beginning should now be made in this improvement which the harbour needs, and which I have several times urged on the minister to carry out. I trust that with the additional information which I have given him, he will see his wax clear to do a reasonable amount of dredging at that port.

I can only say, as I said before to my hon. friend, that I will give the matter my best consideration. If it were possible to do what is called the necessary work at a reasonable expense, Mr. SPROULE.
without engaging in the larger scheme, I would be in a different position. Sometimes, when I have done a certain amount of dredging at a particular place, I am told that I should have gone a certain distance, and that unless I carry the work to completion what has been done will be wasted. I want to look carefully into the matter of dredging the mouth of the channel; I cannot say what will be done; but I will give it my very best consideration.
I am asking that this government redress the injury dohe by a former Liberal government as a beginning,
Is it the minister's intention that this increase in the vote will be spent at the head of the lakes?
This has nothing to do with the expenditure at the head of the lakes. That is a special vote on capital account.

Yes.
