I think we have a special vote for Goderich; I should not take that in. At Hamilton we expect to spend $15,000 this year, Kincardine, $24,000; Lion's Head, $24,000; Meaford, $25,000; Port Bur well, Port Elgin, Port Hope, River Thames, Rondeau channel.
Has the minister the amounts that he expects to spend at each of these points?

These are amounts which have been given as estimates, but I cannot say that we will expend them. Port Bur-well $7,800. I do not want to give that figure with confidence, because the engineers have gone into the matter carefully and I think it is going to cost a great deal more than that.
Can you give us the basis upon which this estimate has been made up?

It has been made up by the clerk who makes up these amounts from estimates given by the. engineering department as to what wo,-k is urgently needed at these places. But when we get into the work we might have to change our estimate very considerably. Then, there are Rondeau, Sarnia, Point Edward, Telegraph island, Nigger island, Wiarton, Waubaushene, Thessalon, Wingfield Basin, Oakville, Owen Sound, Whitby and quite a number of other places along the lakes.
Are all these harbours owned by the government?
Not all owned by the government, but they axe public harbours.
Does my hon. friend expect that any portion of this amount will be expended on harbours that are not owned by the government?

None, unless it might be that we might do something at Port Credit. I have not shut the door against it. Then, in Quebec there are Chateauguay, Chicoutimi, Rimouski, River Batiscan, Riviere du Loup en Haut, Riviere du Loup en Bas, Fraserville, Louisville, River God-froi, River Jesus, River L'Assomption, River Maskinonge, River Nicolet, River St. Francis, St. Frangois du Lac Landing, River St. Maurice mouth, River Saguenay, River Yamache, River Yamaska, St. Pierre Becquets, St. Placide, Three Rivers, and other places. There is dredging work required at Valleyfield, and also at St. Louis river. I am not prepared to give all the different places at the present time. We will not be able to do nearly all the dredging that has been applied for, and which has been urgently recommended by the resident engineers. We will require the amount we are now asking m order to do
a reasonable amount of work with the government dredges, and by contract during the coming season.
Will the minister state where he intends to spend this money in the maritime provinces?
I went into that the other evening. There is no need of my repeating it now, because the hon. gentleman will find it in ' Hansard.*
I think he mentioned some places, but he was not prepared to give all the places at which there might be an expenditure.

I named a large number of places where dredging is required, but I said that I was not able to name all the places. I am not yet able to name them all. We cannot hope to overtake all the work during the present year.

No, but when the minister is asking $675,000 for the maritime provinces that proposed appropriation must be based on some estimate in the department. I do not suppose that the officers of his department go at it blind in striking an estimate of $675,000, just as their fancy may dictate, but it must be based upon a supposed requirement. I would suppose that that requirement must also be based upon the details of the expenditure proposed at different places. * I think it would greatly assist the committee if the minister would give that information. I can hardly conceive that it does not exist.

With respect to the different places where dredging is required we have Teports made of the estimated quantities, and from these reports we ask for a certain amount for dredging. The amount we are asking for we know will not do the work at all these places.

I know, but would not the officer say something like this: Here are twenty-five places; well, there are twenty of them in which we must do dredging to a certain amount at this place; and so he would arrive at the estimate of $675,000? I cannot understand how that estimate is arrived at unless it be by some such method as that or by mere rule of thumb.
It is neither one nor the other.
Well, what is it?

Take the dredging required in the provinces of Ontario, and Quebec to-day, and which might with advantage be undertaken in the public interest, and I am sure it would run up to sev-* eral millions of dollars. But, we cannot

do all that at once. Therefore,. I endeavour to get from my colleagues as much as I can. We have asked for $675,000, and we will have to use this in the places where it is most urgently required in the public interest. If my hon. friend will look through the newspapers he will see that we are advertising for dredging in Ontario, and Quebec, specifying the different places where work is to be done this year.

I do not think the minister has misunderstood although one would almost gather from his remarks that he had. I thoroughly understand that a great many millions of dollars are probably required for dredging purposes in Quebec, and in the maritime provinces and that the work must be performed in the next ten or fifteen years. But I am not talking now about the cost of work to be done in the next fifteen years; I am talking about this year for which an appropriation of $675,000 is asked, and I am asking what seems to me to be an obvious question-at what places do you propose to expend that, and how much do you propose to expend at each place? I suppose that the appropriation must be based on gome estimate of that kind? If it is not based on an estimate of that kind I will venture to suggest that it must be upon the rule to which I have already alluded.

I did not mean by the statement I made that this dredging at these different places would not be required for a number of years. What I intended to say was that if we were to undertake to do the work in the different places in Ontario and Quebec, in which at this very moment it would be desirable to do dredging in the public interest it would run up to two or three, or perhaps four times the amount that we_^ are now asking.

I did not say that at all. I said that you might profitably expend perhaps $10,000,000 in dredging this year, but you are doing only $675,000 worth. Where are you going to do it, and how much are you going to expend in each place?
I could give that to my hon. friend to-night because the advertisements for dredging in Ontario and Quebec are actually out.
I would like to have it.
If the minister would furnish the same information in regard to the maritime provinces, I would be very glad.
I have not it for the maritime provinces. We are working at it, but we have not, it completed. It will be ready some time next week.
I would like the minister to produce that before the estimates are brought up again.
Would the ^ninister also bring down a list of the newspapers in which these advertisements are inserted in Ontario?
Probably I could. I can assure my hon. friend they are not inserted in many Conservative papers. In fact, I cannot recall any at the moment.
Perhaps I could make it easier if I asked my hon. friend to supply the committee with a list of the Conservative papers in which it is inserted.
I will give that to-night. I think it will be a plain sheet of white paper with no mark on it.
The minister has not brought down the information asked with regard to some scows hired from the government by the Maritime Dredging and Construction Company?
I got the dimensions, but I will be glad to get the other information, I had forgotten about it.

A good deal of objection has been taken to the method of computing the work done by contractors by measuring in the scows, and some people think that the measurements might be made in the ground originally staked out requiring excavation to a certain depth over a certain measured area. If they are measuring by scow, it has been publicly stated in the House that the scows frequently go out with half loads and half measurements, and sometimes without any one making any measurement whatever.

It would be possible to have the survey made so as to take the measurements in situ, but with the dredging of harbours and rivers, which is done by the Public Works Department, that would involve a great deal of additional labour and expense at the outset. It is done in the Railway Department, in canal work, but there, of course, the dredging is confined to a narrow and well-defined space, and it can be done much more easily than it could be in ordinary harbour and river work. In Tegard to my hon. friend's statement that it is stated that in many cases scows go out with half a load and that there is no proper measurement,
I have heard that statement made, but I have never heard it verified
We have had one very distinct case.

By any one who pretended to know anything about it? I have never heard that any quantities were paid for which were not actually placed in

scows. It may be that that has occurred in some cases, but we are taking every precaution to prevent it. While, no doubt, there would be some advantages in measuring in situ, there would be difficulties in connection with it in river and harbour work, where the areas cannot be as well defined as in canal work.

A great deal of it seems to be mere guess work when measurement is done on the scow. Whose judgment prevails as to the quantity on a scow? Take the case cited from the Midland district where the inspector is an employee of the scow company, paid partly by the scow company and partly by the government.

That is not the case.
Mr, SPROULE. That was the case brought out under oath right in the Public Accounts Committee.
There might be one case of that kind, but the man would be dismissed the moment it was discovered.
It was brought out as well that he was not on the dredge at all for an hour or two in the morning. Who measured the scows then? Somebody. It is these things that create suspicion.

In the case referred to, the inspector wras employed by the dredging company in the winter making some repairs on a dredge; he was not employed by them in the summer. Even that might be considered improper, as it might tend to favouritism. Ordinarily we believe the inspectors do their duty thoroughly well, and, as I have said, we require that the returns must be made under solemn declaration, which is just the same as making them under oath. In one or two instances where the inspectors were not careful they were instantly dismissed the moment the matter came to the notice of the department.

I gave that one case, and my remembrance of it is that the man was employed not only in the winter, but in the summer as well. Then there is another case where an inspector was walking around the city in hotels, etc., while the scow was working. How was the inspection made then?
Where was that?
It was in Owen Sound, and yet that was said to be correctly and properly done.

That would be said to be most improperly done and the man would be dismissed instantly.
Manitoba, $26,250.

This is to provide for dredging work in the province of Manitoba.
The dredging there is done by a plant owned by the government, and this is for the purpose of operating that plant.
In what waters will this money be expended?
At the mouth of Red river, where it empties into Lake Winnipeg; also some work is asked for in Lake Manitoba and Lake Winnipegosis.
Have advertisements been published in the newspapers in the province of Manitoba?

There will be none, because this is our own plant.
Dredging-British Columbia, $225,000.

This is for the purpose of operating the government plant in British Columbia. The dredging is to be done on the Fraser river, at Victoria, at Vancouver and at Nanaimo, and a number of other places. There are a number of snag boats working on the Thompson and the Skeena rivers, and dredging will be done upon the Arrow lakes, and probably on the Kootenay and Okanagan lakes. We are also asked to do work on the north arm of the Fraser river.

speechtext: I am afraid I cannot let the hon. member proceed, as the House goes automatically into Committee of Supply, which was interrupted at six o'clock.
Dredging-British Columbia, $225,000.

['I think we shall take up a number of Bills which stand on the order paper. Private Bills have priority and after that we shall deal with a number of minor Bills which stand on the order paper. If we reach Supply my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works will continue. There are several Bills on the order paper which, I think, are hardly controversial and we would like to be able to call up any of them.']
The minister promised to bring to the committee a list of newspapers in the province of Ontario in which the advertisements were inserted for the dredging that i3 to be done next year.

I have the list. While we are on the subject of dredging, I wish to correct an error into which I fell'while discussing the cost of dredging phjnt. I was interrogated as to the cost of the dredge ' Industry ', and I stated that the original price as agreed upon was $150,000, and that then a defect had been found, as we thought, in the boiler under the Canadian Inspection Law, and we then offered to the owners of the dredge to take the dredge if $10,000 were deducted for the boiler, we concluding that it would be desirable, if not necessary, to have a new boiler placed in the dredge. The new boiler cost $9,300, and I stated to the committee that the old boiler belonged to the government. In that I was in error. L learned afterwards from Captain Howden, jthe superintendent of dredging, that when the price of the dredge was reduced by $10,000, which was the estimated cost of the new boiler, he agreed that the owners should receive the old boiler, so that when it was taken out of the dredge it was their property, and not the property of the government. I take this, the earliest opportunity, to correct the error into which I fell. My hon. friend wanted a list of the Conservative newspapers in which these advertisements for tenders were inserted. I shall send it to him.

I would rather my hon. friend made a statement to the committee and it would go down on 'Hansard'. He has handed me what I did not want, and has failed to hand in what I did require. My hon. friend has sent over a blank paper, suggesting that no advertisements have been inserted in Conservative papers in respect to dredgiing. I would rather have a list of the newspapers in which the advertisements have been and are inserted for the dredging during the coming summer.

My hon. friend will remember that at first he wanted that and
afterwards he said the other would do. Finding there were no advertisements inserted in Conservative newspapers, I gave him that.

Although mv hon. friend says that patronage list has been eliminated from his department, it appears ncv advertisements are inserted in Conservative newspapers in Ontario. The list will include all leading Reform newspapers in Ontario. Take for example the city of London. Why does he insert the advertisement in a newspaper with a much smaller circulation and refuse to insert it in the leading newspaper of that city, the 'Free Press', which has admittedly the largest circulation in London or in the western part of Ontario? The ministers seek to leave the impression that the patronage lists have been eliminated, but it is evident from this that in regard to newspapers he has continued the patronage list.

My hon. friend will see when the list is produced that the circul-t ation of these papers is so large that all possible dredging tenderers would have ample notice of the call for tenders and that it would be a waste of public money to have given any wider or fuller advertisement.
The only explanation of the minister's course in the case of London is that he inserts the advertisement in papers supporting the government, unless there is some explanation of which I do not know.

I do not think that a gentleman with the long political experience of my hon. friend desires any explanation. It is not customary for governments to advertise works in newspapers owned and controlled bv their opponents unless it is necessary in order to give publicity.

Does the minister not think it is trifling with the committee to present a blank sheet of paper purporting to give information that the House desires? Some members of the governmenti have declared in this House that the patronage system had disappeared and that) the advertisements for contracts were given to all papers, regardless of their political leanings.

I desire to say that I never made such a statement, and I never heard any such statement made by a member of the government as to advertisements' in newspapers. That I regard as a very different thing from a patronage list. Early in this session, and at all times when I have spoken with reference to it, I have said that if, in my opinion, a sufficiently wide circulation can be given by putting
advertisements in friendly newspapers, I will do that.

The minister said he did not say that in this House. If I am right in my memory, he sat in his seat when the Minister of Railways declared in this House that he selected no newspapers, and that he defied contradiction to the statement that he had given these advertisements to papers indiscriminately, and that it was a good thing. If it was a good thing for the Department of Railways and Canals, it must be an equally good thing for the Department of Public Works. My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) desired to ascertain whether that principle is being carried out, and for that reason he asked questions. Now, had it been carried out, and had a list been brought down showing that those advertisements had appeared in a number of Conservative newspapers, it would have been conclusive evidence that the principle was being carried out. But the minister did not attempt to carry it out, and he is trifling with the House when he brings down a piece of blank paper and says: I have not got the other list here.
No, I was requested to produce a list of the Conservative papers in which this advertisement appeared.

He was first required to produce a list of all the papers in which these advertisements appeared.
Mr. PUGSLEY, That request was withdrawn, and my hon. friend asked me to bring down a list of the Conservative papers.
No, the minister is wrong, and is going back on his word.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. My hon. friend has used language which is unbecoming a member of this House in regard to myself; he says I have gone back on my word, and insinuates that I have endeavoured to mislead the committee. My hon. friend surely ought to withdraw that.
I have nothing to withdraw, because I was listening to what he said. After six o'clock this list was to be produced, but afterwards the order was changed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) states that the Minister of Public Works has gone back on his word, I think that expression would be out of order.

Surely I ought to be allowed to give the version of my understanding of what the minister said. If he denies it, then I accept his denial. I have given my understanding of what he said, but he afterwards suggested the change, and the member for Peel innocently fell Mr. PUGSLEY.
into it and accepted it, assuming that the principle was being carried out in its entirety; and if that list had been brought down showing that the advertisement had appeared in a number of Conservative newspapers, the fact would be self-evident.

If, as a matter of fact, these advertisements did not appear in any Conservative newspaper, and if the member for Peel did ask me to bring down a list of Conservative papers in which the advertisements appeared, could I do anything else than give him a blank sheet, if I desired to give correct information to the House?

I think it was beneath the dignity of any minister of the Crown to mislead any member of this House. Knowing as he did that there were no such papers, he should have been frank enough to tell the House so, and that would have obviated the necessity of bringing down a blank,sheet. By refusing to put these advertisements in leading Conservative newspapers, the minister has caused the country to suffer loss. He gave us to understand some time ago that that system was all changed, and several ministers took credit to themselves for introducing a new and better system. Both the Minister of Railways and Canals and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, or the acting minister, gave the country to understand that they had turned over a new leaf, but now we find that they are still adhering to the old and vicious practice, to the loss and detriment of the public service.
The minister rather questioned my statement when I said that the dredging advertisement appeared in only one of the leading newspapers in the city of London.
No, I said I did not know myself in what paper it appeared, and I took my hon. friend's statement as being in effect that he had seen it.

I have before me a copy of the London ' Advertiser ' of March 31. in which I find the advertisement: ' Tenders for dredging-Sealed tenders addressed to the undersigned,' &c. Now, that is a newspaper in the city of London having a fair circulation. I have before me the other leading newspaper of London, the ' Free Press,' which has a very much larger circulation, which is found in almost every home in London and western Ontario. In that newspaper I do not find the advertisement, therefore, I had 'the right to assume that it did not, and does not, appear in the leading newspaper of London, but it does appear in the newspaper that supports the government of my hon. friend.
And which is a leading newspaper.

Which is a leading newspaper. Then my hon. friend admits that there is still a patronage list in his department, no matter what may be found in the Department of Railways and Canals? Therefore, we are to understand that the policy of my hon. friend in the future will be, as in the past, to seek out papers that support his government in the province of Ontario, and put them on the patronage list. But any newspaper that does not support this government, no matter how important it may be, will not be given an advertisement by his department. Might 1 suggest to my hon. friend that - he should take a lesson out of the book of his colleague, the Minister of Railways and Canals, who rather boastingly announced on the floor of the House that a new departure had taken place in his department? How does my hon. friend explain that it is a good thing to abolish the patronage list in the Railway Department and not in my hon. friend's department?

I think that the patronage list, as we all understand it, has been abolished in the Department of Public Works, fust as it has been abolished in the Department of Railways and Canals. I was not here when my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals made the statement which he is alleged to have made, but I must assume that if he did make the statement that advertisements were published in newspapers representing both sides of politics he was referring to special advertisements, such as the time tables on the Intercolonial railway, where it is desirable to give widespread information to the mass of the people. That is a very different thing from publishing advertisements which were intended to reach tlis eyes of contractors. The contractors follow pretty generally the advertising matter contained in all the leading newspapers, and advertising for tenders in more vhfin two or three of the leading newspapers the city of Toronto, for instance, in papers like the Toronto 'Globe,' which has a wide *circulation all over Ontario, and, indeed. I may say all over Canada, and in a number of other leading newspapers in the province where the contracting work is done, gives ample noticei, and it would really be a waste of money to extend the matter further and advertise in papers which are opposed to the government. It is easy for my hon. friend to make these hypocritical speeches, but he knows that if he were in my position to-morrow he would not put a single advertisement in a Liberal newspaper. I know that just as well as my hon. friend does.
How does the hon. gentleman know it?

I know it from my hon. friend's appearance. I know it by the
satirical look that the hon. gentleman has in his face, the look of a man who is trying to take a rise out of his fellow man. I know my hon. friend is just joking when he suggests that we should advertise every ordinary contract, such as dredging work and the erecting of a building, in the opposition newspapers. If it should happen that in any locality we could not give an advertisement sufficiently large circulation through friendly papers we would feel it due to the public to give the advertisement to the newspapers of our opponents.

It is humiliating to hear such a statement from a minister of the Crown. There is no use of mincing the matter; he states plainly that he has made up his mind that he will not advertise in a Conservative newspaper. The hon gentleman must know that if he carries out this policy he cannot do justice to the public, that the people who are reading the Conservative newspapers are perhaps half of the people of Canada, and if he wants to get the best tenders for the work which he is going to undertake he should advertise in the papers that would be likely to be read by the bulk of the people instead of by a small class. At five o'clock this afternoon I received from the office upstairs a return showing the amount of money that this government is expending on newspapers all over the country. I have not had time to go over it, and I do not see amongst these papers a statement of the money expended by the Department of Public Works. I shall expect to see it, however, before the return can be considered complete. What I asked for, as far as the Department of Public Works is concerned,, was an order of the House showing the total amount paid in each year since 1896 for all printing and advertising done outside of the government printing bureau. Last year the Department of the Interior expended $167,404.84 for advertising in newspapers, not altogether in Canada. This money was distributed amongst nearly 700 firms or newspapers. Perhaps 600 of them would be in Canada. The minister may think that that is a splendid position for the Minister of the Interior to take.
It has helped to produce splendid results in the way of immigration.

Yes, but how much better might these results have been had that money been distributed in a nonpartisan way instead of in the way the minister would advise the money to be distributed? The same department, for printing, distributed $95,393 to practically the same firms as my hon. friend might see if he went over the list. For lithographing they paid out $4,509. In that department,

$267,307 and $11,620 were expended for foreign printing and advertising. The bulk of that sum was expended in the Dominion of Canada. For what purpose? For the purpose of influencing-may I say-the press of this country, and if you look through the returns which I have here you will find that practically every dollar of that money went to the Liberal press of this country. How can you expect that the Liberal press is going to do justice to what is transpiring on the floor of this House if you are going to give them,, for advertising, printing and lithographing, $500,000 per annum, making a rough estimate? There is $500,000 per annum going to buy up, to a certain extent,, the Liberal press, and according to the statement of the Minister of Public Works to-night, none of the Conservative newspapers may expect, unless they will truckle and bow the knee to this government, that they will get one dollar of the money that is being expended. Is that a statesmanlike position for a minister of the Crown to take? I cannot conceive that one in his position can feel that he is doing justice to his department or to the people of Canada in taking the position that he has taken to-night, and I am surprised to hear him make such a statement. I sincerely hope that before the session closes I may be able to show to his satisfaction that he is neglecting his duty as n minister when he arrogates to himself the right to say that he will distribute the people's money to the press that will support his government, no matter what kind of trickery and corruption they may carry on. I am satisfied that when the people realize that $500,000 of their money is going into the ink pots of the government to bolster up their position they will resent it as well as the statement that he made to-night, that he will not advertise in one of the opposition papers.

Prior to 1896, did the hon. gentleman ever see a government advertisement in a Liberal newspaper? Has he during the past three or four years seen an Ontario government advertisement in a Liberal newspaper?
Yes, sir, the Ontario government advertises in the Toronto Globe.
That is the only instance.

Not at all, they are advertising in other Liberal newspapers. But why should gentlemen opposite be continually bringing up what happened before 1896. If the Conservative government erred then, is that any reason why to-day $500,000 of the money of the people should year after year be turned over to Liberal newspapers in Canada, and as Mr. ARMSTRONG.
every one knows, the minute any one of these newspapers says a word against the government they are shut off from participation in the funds. The minister knows very well that in the city of Halifax gov-emmrfru patronage has been withdrawn from Liberal newspapers that said anything against the government,
I know nothing of the kind.
Why, the minister has told us that if a paper does not support the government it need not expect a dollar in the way of printing.
I have not said that.
The minister has not said it in so many words, but that is the inference from his remarks.

The Minister of Public Works stated that only time-tables, and so on, were advertised by the Department of Railways in the Conservative newspapers, but as a matter of fact, advertisements for supplies for the Intercolonial are published in the Conservative newspapers. The Minister of Railways told us that he believed it good policy to advertise in all the newspapers, and he intended to do it, and I believe the acting Minister of Marine does the same thing.
Does the hon. gentleman not think it would be looked upon as a huge joke all over the country if they saw a Liberal government advertising in Conservative newspapers.
I am not here to judge of jokes now.

If I were to express an opinion on this matter I would differ from the Minister of Public Works, as well as from the hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong). I do not think that any of us on this side are expecting that the Conservative press should receive any large amount of patronage from the present government, but I do believe that the government would find it a better plan if tenders were advertised for through the 'Canada Gazette,' and if the advertisements were not published in any newspapers, either Conservative or Liberal. If my suggestions were carried out the contractors would all look to the ' Canada Gazette ' for such advertisements, and if the government adopted that system it would be more satisfactory all round. But what I rose to speak about was another matter. The minister was good enough to mention Oakville, in the county of Halton, as one of the places where dredging would be done this summer. As we have passed into the fiscal year 1911, the money is now available for that work, and I would impress upon the minister the great necessity of having the dredging done at Oakville as

early as possible. It is not possible for the steamers passing from Toronto to Hamilton to call at Oakville harbour at present, and it is very desirable that whatever dredging is to be done should be done early in the season. Can the hon. gentleman tell us when we may expect a* government dredge at Oakville?

I am fully seized of the importance of the work at Oakville, but I regret that I cannot say just when the dredge will be sent there. We have numerous demands from different sections of Ontario, but I may say to my hon. friend that we intend to have the work done at Oakville as soon as possible.
Slides and booms-Saguenay district-new booms, alligator tug, and additional equipment, $10,000.
How much of this is for booms, and how much for the tug?
It is estimated that the tug will cost $3,500, the booms $5,000 and $1,500 for chains and such appliances.
What is the capacity of an alligator tug that will cost $3,500?
I do not know, but I am informed that that is about what we paid for one previously.
I have one of the largest alligator tugs made, and I can tell my hon. friend that I never had to pay for such a tug within $1,000 of what he estimates.
What is your alligator tug worth?
What is the capacity.
Fifty horse-power, and 1 think 62 feet long. I am doubtful if the minister knows what an alligator tug is?
The minister knows more than you think.
What is it?
An alligator tug is a tug that goes over land and water; is that right?
Quite right.
Who manufactures tugs in Canada?

I am unable to say. Mr. Howden, the superintendent of dredging, purchased the last one. Of course we will get it at the lowest price possible.
St. Maurice district-improvements to slide and boom works, &c., $40,000.
Extensive pulp mills and other large manufacturing establishments on the St. Maurice river render these improvements absolutely essential.
Are these cedar booms?

Some; we use a good deal of British Columbia fir in them. They will be, speaking generally, 3 or 4 ply storage booms.
Chapeau bridge over the Culbute channel of the Ottawa river, $25,000.

There was an appropriation of $15,000 made for this work at the last session of parliament, 'but we did' not use it. We have now let the contract, and we require this $25,009 to make payment. The province of Quebec contributes $5,000 towards the bridge.
Is it a new structure?
Yes, a traffic bridge
It is in the province of Quebec, I understand?

It is to all intentions and purposes an interprovincial bridge. It is to replace an old bridge which -was built 40 years ago by the federal government and has been repaired from time to time since by that government. The Ottawa river at that point forms the boundary between the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. It happens that the Culbute channel over which the bridge is built is actually in the province of Quebec; but the other channel is in the province of Ontario, and there is a ferry from the island to the Ontario side, so that it is all one system of interprovincial communication.

I am not objecting to it, because if it is an interprovincial bridge, I think that fact would justify the expenditure; but I do not think the minister has admitted the principle that we should erect bridges over streams unless they are required for railways or something like that.

The principle has been admitted for many years of constructing with federal money bridges which connect two provinces. In some cases the provincial authorities contribute and in some cases they do not.
I admit that the federal government have granted subsidies, but I do not think they have taken the responsibility of building these bridges themselves.

Yes, there are two or three on the Ottawa river which have been built by the federal government, including the Chaudiere bridge at Ottawa.
Courtenay bay-Marsh road-to provide for one-third of cost of rebuilding aboiteau on road to protect marsh and Intercolonial railway property at St. John, New Brunswick, the remaining two-thirds of cost to be contributed by provincial government and city of St. John, $8,000.

This work is to be carried out by the city of St. John, and the cost is to be borne jointly by that city, the provincial government and the federal government, as all three bodies are interested-the city by reason of the bridge being within the city limits, the provincial government by reason of its being interested in the marsh road, which is a public highway, and the Dominion government by reason of the fact that the aboiteau prevents the tide flowing over the marsh and the Intercolonial railway property.
Are public tenders invited for this work?
Yes, by the city of St. John, which has awarded the contract accordingly, and when it completes the work we will pay our one-third.
Has my hon. friend's department any inspection over the work?

No. It is being done entirely by the city of St. John.
International bridge across the River St. John, between St. Leonard, New Brunswick, and Van Buren, Maine, the state of Maine contributing an equal amount, $37,500.

This is to construct a bridge which is very much needed in the public interest, as there is a great, deal of intercourse carried on ferries at this point. The legislature of the state of Maine has passed a law engaging to contribute one-half the cost of this bridge, and we have thought it advisable in the public interest to contribute the other half.
Is this an ordinary traffic bridge or a railway bridge?
It is an ordinary traffic bridge, and is to be free.
Under which government is it constructed?

It is to be constructed under a joint arrangement between the Department of Public Works here, and the Public Works Department of the state of Maine.
Interprovincial bridge across River Ottawa at Hawkesbury; the Ontario and Quebec governments to contribute each $15,000, $50,000.
This bridge has been pressed upon our attention for a considerable time as being very necessary in the public interest. The total probable cost is $116,300.
Who has charge of the construction?
The Public Works Department.
This will be another free traffic bridge?

Yes.
Interprovincial bridge over Restigouche river at Metapedia; the local governments of Quebec and New Brunswick each to contribute $5,000, $25,000.
Mr. PUGiSLEY. Out of this vote we will use $14,705 to pay the Department of Railways for the iron that goes into the superstructure, and the balance will be used towards making a payment on the contract for the bridge.
What is the total estimated cost?
$62,705. It is a steel bridge with stone substructure.
This is going to be a free bridge too, I suppose?

Yes.
Ottawa city-bridges over the Ottawa river, the slides and the Rideau canal and approaches thereto-ordinary repairs and renewals and maintenance, $12,000.
This is the usual amount required to make the ordinary repairs to the four bridges which we maintain.
Does the government maintain all bridges over the canal?
Not all. The city of Ottawa has some bridges. I think these four bridges are all the government maintain. Of course the Railway Department may maintain some over the canal.
Why do you maintain some bridges and not others?

The Chaudiere bridge over the Ottawa is interprovincial. Some of the bridges over the canal were built many years ago by the government, and in 1882 an agreement was entered into by the late government that the government *should maintain these bridges; the government has recognized its obligations and has maintained them. As to new bridges which the city might construct a new rule would apply.
The Laurier bridge?

That was built by government 35 or 40 years ago, and replaced ten years ago.
Dominion traffic bridges throughout Canada, including approaches generally, $5,000.
This is the usual vote to repair works of this character for which there is no special vote.

I thought it was the policy of the government not to contribute anything towards bridges except to companies, that is, not to contribute to provincial government bridges. I understood

the minister took that stand in reference to bridge matters in British Columbia some time ago, but it is evident that the government have assumed financial responsibility-on a lot of provincial bridges which the provincial governments have been partially assisting, the great burden of the expense falling on the Federal government. I would like the minister to explain that in reference to his refusal to grant assistance in the British Columbia case some years ago. I think the matter came up in reference to the New Westminster bridge.

British Columbia in this respect has been treated exactly the same as the other provinces of Canada, there has been no distinction. There have been applications from Ontario and other provinces. I think I remember an application from British Columbia and others from other provinces of Canada, but the government, ever since Confederation, has taken the view that where a bridge is wholly within a province, and cannot in any sense be regarded as interprovincial, it would not recognize that bridge as a Federal work or one that ought to be attended to by the Federal government, but rather that it was a matter for the provincial governments or municipalities to look after. In the case of interprovincial bridges a different view has prevailed. The practice ever since confederation has been for the Federal government to build interprovincial bridges, bridges across rivers connecting two provinces, or in some cases connecting Canada with the United States, the river being a boundary river. All these bridges for which votes have been asked to-night are interprovincial or international bridges. In that respect they differ entirely from the bridge at New Westminster, crosisng the Fraser river, which would be wholly within the province of British Columbia.'
Telegraph lines on north shore and islands of Lower St. Lawrence, &c.-improvement of repair service, $3,000.
What is the nature of this line?

It is very necessary for the Signal Service with reference to shipping, the weather reports, etc., but the country is not sufficiently thickly settled to make this a good commercial undertaking. The revenue in the province of Quebec last year was $11,168.80.
There are other lines besides this?
Yes.
What was the expenditure?
$31,965, that is outside altogether of the services of the cable ship.
Is the revenue increasing, and the expenditure decreasing?

It is keeping just about the same on each side.
Telegraph lines-Alberta and Saskatchewan, Edmonton-Athabaska telegraph lines-extension from Athabaska Landing towards Peace River Landing, via south side of Lesser Slave lake, $21,000.
This is to extend the telegraph service from Edmonton to the north. A good many settlers are going into the Peace river country, and need a telegraph service.
How.far did you extend this line last year?
About 140 miles. It is 290 miles long altogether.
If you did 140 miles last year with $10,000, why do vou want $25,000 to do the balance?

I should have said in the two years. In 1908 and 1909 we spent nearly $10,000, and during the year which closed.yesterday we spent $10,'l94. With this amount we ought to be able to finish it this year.
Moosejaw - Wood Mountain line-branch from Limerick to Gravelburg, $5,000.
Are these lines constructed by public competition?
We supply the wire ourselves, and put up the line, but we call for tenders for the poles. The construction is done by men employed under our own superintepdence.
Would it not be better to ask for tenders for poles and wires, and construct the line?

It is well to ask for tenders for poles, but I think the work can be done better and more cheaply by our own men. I think that is the way the telegraph companies construct their lines, they have their own crews.
Are the rates fixed on the expenditure?	-
We endeavour to fix them based somewhat upon the expenditure, but usually in comparison with what the companies charge on lines similarly situated.
What is the total revenue and expenditure on all the government telegraph lines?
The total revenue last vear was $113,175; the total expenditure, including the Yukon, was $474,845.
Are there any telegraph lines in Ontario?
We have only one, the Pelee Island Tine, that is a telephone line.
Have there never been any applications for such lines in the outlying portions of Ontario?
Not since I have been minister.

I want to know how these things are done. Is it by application made by certain municipalities or individuals, and what are the conditions on which grants of that kind are made? I know some outlying districts, for instance in my own riding, which are thirty-five or forty miles from a railway, and a good way from telephone lines. Now is there any possibility that the people of these districts would be'able to get a grant to assist them in building those lines?

While there is no absolute rule, yet the principle upon which the government began to. act a great many years ago was that it was desirable in the public interest to give telegraphic communication to outlying, and remote sections of the country, more especially in the newer provinces, and in unsettled districts where lines would not likely be built by commercial companies. As to whether an application for a telephone or telegraph line in a well settled district, which is blessed by the presence of my hon. friend, should be granted I would have very grave doubts. I would hardly think that my hon. friend would seriously propose the construction of a line in a locality such as that. But out in British Columbia, in the thinly settled districts, in the Yukon, in the mountains, away down on the lower St. Lawrence, and in districts like that where there is no reasonable hope that at any time in the near future commercial companies will enter the field, the government is giving accommodation to the people.
. Mr. U. WILSON. I have not made myself clear to the hon. gentleman. He has described the conditions in that part of the country to which I am referring where they have no telegraph or telephone lines, where the country is sparsely settled, and the people are put to great inconvenience. This district is about ninety miles north of the county town. They have a cheese factory, and they cannot keep in touch with the prices unless they have telephonic or telegraphic communication. It is hardship enough that they have to draw their cheese thirty-five or forty miles to the railway station in order to get it to market, and if anything could be done to facilitate them in getting the market reports such as this government is doing for other localities, it seems to me that they have a strong claim.

I suppose my hon. friend would not have any fear that the Mr. PUGSLEY.
question of provincial rights would be raised at once if the Dominion sought to invade that territory by building a telegraph or telephone line?

I do not think that would trouble the Minister of Public Works very much. If it suited his purpose I think he would go on irrespective of provincial rights.	.
Telegraph lines, British Columbia-North Thompson Valley line-land line, Kamloops to Fennels-revote of lapsed amount, $4,500.
This is to construct a telephone line from Kamloops to Fennels on the north side of the Thompson river, sixty miles in length.
How much has been constructed?
There cannot be a great deal, because we have only expended $446.41.
Is it expected to go on with the work?

Yes, we expect to build sixty miles this year. .
Kamloops-Okanagan Valley telephone line - additional wiring between Kelowna and Penticton and overhauling and strengthening line, $7,600.
This line is 42h miles in length, and it will cost $160 a mile.
That is rewiring.
We want to give a separate circuit independent of the telegraph system. This work has been asked for by the Penticton Board of Trade, and recommended by our superintendent there.
Are we to understand that this is a very sparsely settled district?
Yes, it is. My hon. friend from British Columbia (Mr. Burrell) would know better about it than I. The section is beginning to fill up rapidly.
Communication is partly by road, and partly by water, and the situation is extremely difficult.
You will go many miles there without seeing a house?

There was a matter that I brought to the attention of the minister last December that I would like to mention again. I would like to know whether it is possible to have an extension of the Okanagan system or rather to construct a branch from Kamloops over to the Okanagan away entirely from the railway system and over a country that is never likely to be reached by the railway.
Is that from Kamloops?

Yes. From Kamloops, passing through Duck's, Grand Prairie, Glenemma, Faulkland, and Hullcar to the Armstrong district. That is a country in the railway belt that is beginning to be settled and where a large number of people can be served in no other way than by a telephone line. I hope the minister has taken that into his favourable consideration and I trust that there will be a possibility of having that line constructed at the earliest possible date.

I am impressed with the desirability of this work. I think my attention was called to it by Senator Bos-toek some time ago. As I understand this will give a short cut across the country and give accommodation to a large number of people. Recognizing the possibility that there will be some supplementary estimates I have had this line noted and I am not without hope that I may succeed in getting an appropriation for the purpose and that the work will go ahead this season.
The condition of the settlefs in that district appeals to me, but I understand this work would be quite expensive, as the country is very mountain ous.

It is not so mountainous there.
Mr. PUGSLEY7. I can tell my hon. friend (Mr. Burrell) that his remarks about the settlers will have my earnest consideration, and it is only the question of expense that would deter me from taking necessary steps to extend the line in that direction.

I do not wish to be understood as objecting to such expenditure as this, but I do impress on the minister that we have in the province of Ontario numerous instances which are just as much entitled to receive assistance of this kind. In many places in eastern Ontario, the country is Tough and sparsely settled, and there is no inducement for a private company to undertake a telephone or telegraph service. The people are badly in need of such a service, and I may tell the minister that in all probability he will have applications in this direction pressed upon him in the near future.
Kamloops-Okanagan Y'alley telephone line, exchange at Merritt, $2,250.
I suppose that this work will be gone on with this summer?

Yes.
National Art Gallery, Ottawa, including the purchase of paintings by the Advisory Council of Art, $10,000.
How are these pictures purchased?

By the Advisory Art Council, which did consist of the late Sir George Drummond, Mr. Byron Walker and Senator Boyer. On the death of Sir George Drummond, Dr. Shepherd, a very eminent surgeon of Montreal, and who is, I believe, a very good judge of paintings, kindly consented to take the vacancy. These gentlemen give the benefit of their judgment and knowledge to the country free of charge.
Monument to the memory of the late Hon. George Brown, $10,000.
Where will this monument be placed?
In Ottawa, but we have not yet determined on the locality.

You have been neglecting the memory of this gentleman for many

years. Why was nothing done when the money was voted last year?

The sculptor is at work, but we did not make any payment last year.
Monument to the memory of the late Hon. Thomas D'Arcy McGee, $10,000.

Can the minister say whether this statue will be placed on Parliament hill, or near the Laurier hotel. I see the volunteers' monument is to-day placed at the rear oi the hotel, and I impe these statues will not be given any such \ site as that.

These monuments will be located on the advice of the Advisory Art Council. It is rather believed by myself and the members of the government generally that the monument of the late Thomas D'Arcy McGee will be placed on the proposed plaza which is to be built between the two bridges, opposite the station and hotel.

I suppose that D'Arcy McGee being an Irishman, you are following the example of the city of Dublin which placed the statue of Daniel O'Connell in the middle of Sackville street. But, I should think that the services rendered by D'Arcy McGee entitled his statue to a better location than in the middle of a street.
The new statue of Shakespeare, one of the finest in Paris, is right in the middle of a street.
Well, I am not sure that it is always safe to take Paris as a model.
The statute of Lincoln in New York is in the middle of a street.

I never was in New York, and I only speak of what I know. It is quite possible that the statue may be placed in the middle of a street, but for my part I would rather see the monument of McGee on Parliament hill.
The plaza will be very beautiful, and I think it will be a good location for that statue.
I think we should follow the example of some of these eminent statesmen and not talk so much, and let us get through the business of the House.
I did not hear what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Black) said; did he reflect in any way on the statement I made?
Not at all. I think Thomas D'Arcy McGee was entitled to whatever honour we can do him.

Notwithstanding what the hon. member (Mr. Black) says, I Mr. BLAIN.
think this is a matter of sufficient importance to occupy us for a few moments. The name of Thomas D'Arcy McGee is inseparably connected with the history of Canada, and he is -worthy of any honour we can confer upon his memory. In view of the political services of Thomas D'Arcy McGee to Canada and his high position as a statesman, it seems to me that his statue should be erected upon Parliament hill.

In suggesting that D'Arcy McGee's statue should be erected on the plaza opposite the post office, there was no ! idea that it would be in any less distinguished position than if it were erected on Parliament hill. For example, in London, on Parliament square, which is across from the parliament buildings, there are a great number of monuments of the most din-tinguished men in the history of the empire. There are at present a good many monuments on Parliament hill, and in my view it is quite possible that the plaza opposite the post office, being in the most frequented part of the capital of the Dominion, is a no less distinguished position. I quite agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) that Thomas D'Arcy McGee was one of the most distinguished men in the history of our country, and that the tragic manner in which he met his death in consequence of one of the most patriotic stands that ever a statesman took in the history of Canada, entitles his memory to the highest repect we can pay.

I am afraid that if the hon. minister carries out his intention he may find himself somewhat in the position of the tourist, who, when driving around the Lakes of Killarney, asked the cabman what was the height of a particular monument, and the cabman replied: 'I think it is the height of damn nonsense to put it there,, because I run against it every time I drive around it.'
Monument to the memory of the late Sir L. H. Lafontaine and the late Robert Baldwin, $20,000.
Is it the intention of the government to honour other Canadian statesmen, and if so, to what extent?
I should think that from time to time it would be the duty of this government or of any government which might be in power to do honour in the same way to other eminent statesmen.
Is it likely to include the men of to-day?
The Minister of Public Works, for instance.

I would rather hope that my hon. friend would become so distinguished in the service of his country that he would be deemed by the govern-

ment of his country worthy of a high place on parliament hill or on the plaza.
Grant towards the erection of a memorial at or near Brantford to commemorate the invention of the telephone, $5,000.
How much are these monuments expected to costr
The amount fixed in the contract for the monument for Hon. Geo. Brown is $10,000. It is expected that this monument at Brantford will cost about $40,000. Our contribution will not exceed $10,000.
Of the other monuments, the government is bearing the whole ccst?
Yes.
If $10,000 will build each of the other monuments, how does this one come to cost $40,000?

We have nothing to do with that. The people of Brantford, taking a pride in their fellow-citizen,, Prof. Bell, who invented the telephone, and desirous of erecting a monument in commemoration of his great work, estimate that it will cost about $42,000.
When will it be completed?

I presume that it is very nearly completed, because the secretary of the committee has called on us for the payment of the last half of our contribution.
Contribution towards the erection of a memorial to Sir Leonard Tilley at St. John, New Brunswick, $4,000.

This is being erected by a committee of citizens, who received subscriptions. The provincial government is contributing $2,50(1 and we think it not unreasonable that we should make a contribution of $4,000 towards this monument in memory of one whose public services were so great and who occupied such a commanding position as Sir Leonard Tilley.

I confess that when I read the words, 'a contribution towards the erection of a monument,5 I did not like it. It seemed to me that, considering the great work of Sir Leonard Tilley in this country, he had just as much right to be remembered by this parliament as some of those whose names have been mentioned, and I would have preferred to have seen this government erect a monument to the memory of Sir Leonard Tilley. He has erected a monument for himself, a monument that will last as long as this country lasts.

I ought to explain, for the information of my hon. friend and the
committee, that this work of erecting a monument to Sir Leonard Tilley was taken in hand a few years ago, and it is intended to erect it, not here in the capital of the country, but in the city of St. John; and the chairman of the committee communicated with this government and asked us to make a contribution. We are doing exactly what the committee appeared to prefer that we should do. I think it would not be doing justice to the feelings of the friends of Sir Leonard Tilley if we were to attempt to take the matter out of their hands.
Did they name the amount?
Yes, and we quite fulfilled their expectations as to that; we have even done a little better.

This monument is in Sir Leonard Tilley's own province, but I think he was a man prominent enough in the history of his country, and he did sufficient in his day to entitle his name to be honoured by the erection of a monument here at the capital, where he did his great work, and where he was one of the prominent figures in the .national life of this country.
If the city of St. John is erecting a monument to Sir Leonard Tilley, I think the minister might well consider the propriety of erecting one at the capital.

The matter is worthy of consideration, and I have no doubt the government will carefully weigh the suggestion of my hon. friend.
Construction of water-storage dams and regulation works on the Upper Ottawa river and tributaries, $175,000.

This is to continue the very important work of erecting storage dams upon the head waters of the Ottawa with a view to holding back the flood waters in order to increase the flow of the river Ottawa during the dry season. It will greatly increase the flow past the city, add very largely to the water-power, and greatly improve the navigation.
Is there not plenty of water-power now?
Not at low water.
At what points is it proposed to build?

We are building dams at the foot of Lake Timiskaming, on Lake Keepawa, on Lake Quinze and on two other lakes, and we have under consideration a project of diverting into the Ottawa valley system one of the rivers which now flows northwards. I believe a great increase of flow can be got from that source
What is the whole undertaking expected to cost?

In the vicinity of $600,-
000.
I see that you spent $65,000 in the current year. How has that been spent?
Under contract, after public tender.
And I presume it is intended to spend the money now being voted in the same way.

Yes, on the contracts now let.
Engineering branch-salaries of engineers, inspectors, superintendents, draftsmen, clerks and messengers of outside service, $170,000.
This year we require $25,000 more than we took last year, owing to the increased number of employees, as well as some increases in salaries. The work of the department is growing very rapidly.
What increases in salaries are there?

Will my hon. friend allow me to give him the detail of that at a later date? I haven't it to-night.
Deep Waterways Commission, inclusive of payments authorized to Wm. J. Stewart, chief hydrographic surveyor, Department of Marine and I'isheries, as member of the Board of Commissioners; also for the definition and demarcation of the international boundary between the United States and Canada from Pigeon river to St. Regis, as provided for by article 4 of the treaty of April 11, 1908, $50,000.

I presume the committee are very familiar with the work of the International Waterways Commission. This amount has been asked for by the commission who state that it will be all required during the current year.
What salary does the chairman receive?
Fifty dollars a day for the days he is actually engaged upon the work.	[DOT]
How many days was that last year?
I have not the amounts paid to the different commissioners, but the total amount paid as salaries to all the commissioners, and to the secretary was $9,948.47.

I think the chairman received about $3,000.
International Commission, River St. John, New Brunswick, $20,000.

This is to pay the expenses of a commission sitting jointly with Mr. PUGSLEY
a commission appointed by the government of the United States to consider the question of obstructions to the St. John river, made by a company incorporated by the legislature of the state of Maine. Since the commission was appointed the scope of their inquiry has been enlarged, and they are considering the question of the feasibility of storing waters at the headwaters of the River St. John, and its tributaries with a view to improving navigation, and to see if by means of improving the navigation the injury caused by obstructions, booms and piers, on the American side, might not be obviated or lessened. They are also dealing with the diversion of the waters of the Allegash river from the St. John river into the Penobscot river, which was done some years ago by people in the state of Maine. The work of the commission is very important, and we are asking this amount towards paying their expenses.
Are they considering how far those obstructions are a violation of the Ashburton treaty?
That comes within the scope of their duty.
Have they any power to determine matters that will be binding on their government?

No, their report would not bind the governments, but no doubt it would have''great weight with the two governments, particularly if it should be unanimous. The primary object of the appointment is of course to inquire into all the facts so as to present a full report, which could be relied upon, to the government of the United States, and to the government of Canada.
Lake Nipissing-water level controlling dams -to provide for payment of claims for flooded lands, $10,000.
Is that at the lower end of Lake Nipissing?
Yes.
Has the minister made up his mind as to whether he is going to do that little bit of dredging work over at Wolfe island?
No, I have not,
Would the minister say whether he is likely to make it up in the near future?

That is a difficult question to answer. The work asked for i3 essentially an improvement of private property, dredging immediately in front of a privately owned dock. My hon. friend will see that if I were to do that I would not be free from criticism from his own side of the House, unless he exercised a very

controlling influence over some hon. gentlemen who sit near him.

I think I can give an assurance that he will not be severely criticised from this side of the House. While I do not profess to control members, I think I can give that assurance with every confidence. As to its being a private wharf, the minister is right to a certain extent; it is private owned, but it is used by the public to a very great extent. The advantage to the public would be about sixty cents or seventy cents a ton on all the coal they use. I understand the municipality would go to the expense of putting up a coal shed so that this little bit of dredging, costing $200 or $300, would enable the coal barges to unload right at the wharf. I do not think the minister would be criticised from this side, he certainly would not receive any severe criticism from the people in that locality if he made that expenditure.

While I have every confidence in the good faith of my hon. friend, it would give me more confidence in the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite if I were to hear from the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule) because he is leading the opposition.
I can assure the hon. minister he will not encounter any criticism from the hon. member from Grey regarding it.

We have advanced quite a long distance. I find hon.. gentlemen opposite are quite prepared to support the expenditure of government money on what are absolutely private wharfs, and certainly, that being so, I will be called upon to give the matter even more careful consideration than I have done hitherto. I cannot promise my hon. friend, but I will take the matter into consideration.

I do not wish to raise any objection to this expenditure, but I think the minister is putting a wrong construction on what is said by the member for Grey, and the member for Fronte-nac. What they referred to was this specific case, not generally speaking.
A principle is a principle. If it is good for one case, it is good for another.
Providing the conditions are always alike.
If a wharf is a privately owned wharf.
Used by the public.
Yes, every privately owned wharf is used by the public.
Without tolls, largely without tolls.
Largely without tolls. There is a modification there.
I want to be fair, and I think there have been many instances where grants have been made for which there was less justification than in this case.
Are we to understand that it would be a new departure on the part of my hon. friend if an expenditure of this kind were made?

There would be ground for criticism. It would not be unreasonable that I should be criticised for making improvements to what w'as really a private wharf owned by a private individual, who often collects tolls for the use of that wharf. It is often difficult to diraw the line. There would be criticism in this case, because the work is not a large one, and the public might well say that the owner of this wharf might have this dredging done at his own expense, that it was only a matter of two or three hundred dollars, and why should the government spend public money to improve this property? That is the criticism that would be made. But it has been done in cases where the public receive larger accommodation, as, for instance, improving a channel in front of a railway wharf, there, of course, the interests of the railway company come in, and the transportation interests in which the public is concerned. However, in this case the wharf is owned by a private individual, and he would receive the benefit of the government's expenditure. The amount is not large. I say again in perfect good faith that I am considering the matter, and I have not yet decided whether I can do it or not.
If we can get an assurance, or a written undertaking, from the owner of this wharf, that no toll will be charged to coal vessels, that is to say, that that part of the wharf will be absolutely free-
What about the rest of the traffic?

That is unloaded on a different part of the wharf. I have no doubt the owner of this wharf will sell to the government at a very reasonable figure, yet it is a government owned wharf. It would be rather a unique experience for that part of the country.
No, in Ontario there is a large number of government owned wharfs.	,
My question was as to whether the department has not in the past expended money upon private wharfs in the province of Ontario and other parts of Canada.
I thought I answered that fairly. ^

My hon. friend made an explanation, but failed to touch the point. I will repeat the question. Has not his department in the past expended money upon private wharfs, both in Ontario and in other provinces?
I am not aware of the government expending money on private wharfs in the sense in which this is a private wharf. Would my hon. friend point out a particular instance?
There is a case at Sault Ste. Marie where the government has done dredging in front of a wharf to allow vessels to get up to the wharf.
In that case the wharf was bought by the government, and improvements were made after the government became the owner of the property. That is what the chief engineer tells me.
I can tell both the chief engineer and the minister that money was spent there several times before the wharf was owned by the government.
That might have been under the old administration.
I think there is a case at Orillia, and another in front of Barrie, and I think there is another at Little Current, or some where on the Manitoulin island.

A short time ago I had an application from an owner of a wharf in or near the city of Ottawa to do some dredging, and I said I would do it if the owner would pay so much for the dredging. I think I gave directions to the chief engineer to charge a reasonable price for the work. I happen to have owned, with two or three other gentlemen, a wharf in the city of St. John; we wanted some dredging done by the government, and we had to pay the actual cost of operating the dredge, I think some $40 or $50 a day, while the dredge was doing work in front of this wharf.
Compensation to Sydney J. Dale in full of all demands for injuries sustained by him on the government dredge ' Nakusp,' in June, 1907, whilst employed as deckhand-revote of $500 lapsed, $1,000.

I asked for a vote of $500 in 1908, but Mr. Dale, acting on the advice of his _ friends, declined to accent it. After looking carefully into the circumstances of the case I have decided to recommend a vote of $1,000 to this unfortunate man.
j Mr. EDWARDS. To what extent was he | injured?

When he was working on the dredge 'Naskusp', at Revelstoke, he received such injury to his arm that it had to be amputated. On the occasion of the same accident Captain Baker lost his life. It occurred whilst the crew of the dredge were installing a new main guy line. Of course, the question arose as to whether there was liability on the part of the government and on looking into the whole case and after consulting with the deputy minister and the chief engineer I decided that it would be right to compensate this man to the extent of $1,000.
Do I understand that on looking into the matter you considered the government was liable and that an action for damages might be made good by this'man?

Mr. Dale did commence suit by petition of right and on looking into the matter I thought the case was, at all events, so doubtful as that it would be in the interest of the public that we should make a settlement. I also felt that even if we might defeat the man's claim in a court of law, he had a strong equitable claim. He probably had a legal claim, hut he certainly had a strong moral claim.

I presume this man is the head of a family and that his family depend upon him for their living. If the government considered thev were liable for the damage done to this man I think it is dealing in a pretty small way to give him $1,000 compensation for the loss of his arm. A man's arm ought to be worth more than that to him. It the government are liable at all he should receive more than -$1,000.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up on Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think we shall take up a number of Bills which stand on the order paper. Private Bills have priority and after that we shall deal with a number of minor Bills which stand on the order paper. If we reach Supply my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works will continue. There are several Bills on the order paper which, I think, are hardly controversial and we would like to be able to call up any of them.
